description: OWASP Foundation talks from OWASP Foundation 2025.

talks.title: OWASP Leaders: How to manage your project, chapter, working group, or meeting
talks.teaser: Shows how OWASP project, chapter and working group leaders edit their pages and create meetings on the new website.
talks.summary:
This walkthrough introduces the new OWASP website and explains how leaders sign in to manage their own content. Access begins with a magic link that expires after an hour, followed by a password reset. The presenter notes that passwords are being phased out, with Google single sign-on planned for OWASP staff and passkeys for everyone else. Once signed in, a dashboard lists the projects, working groups and chapters a user can manage.

The middle of the video covers each area in turn. Project leaders use the admin dashboard to edit page content, add or remove leaders, add members, and add links and tabs, and they must click save changes on each tab before moving on. Working group leaders use the manage groups page to add markdown content, and chapter leaders edit their chapter details, such as the leader's name and contact email, with the save button sitting at the bottom of the page. Meetings for any project or chapter are created from an add meeting option, using a title, location, date, time, attendee limit and description.

The closing section covers migration. Chapter content on the old site stays available until the end of the year, after which chapter repositories will be retired. Project repositories that mix page content and code will be split with help from the foundation team. Redirects from old addresses, hidden RSVPs and finer regional groupings are planned, and viewers are invited to send feedback and attend office hours the following week.

talks.title: OWASP Global Board of Directors Public Board Meeting
talks.teaser: Covers board votes, finance figures, sanctions advice, policy reviews and committee status at OWASP's public board meeting.
talks.summary:
The OWASP Foundation's global board holds its public meeting. Directors vote on the agenda order and approve the June and July minutes. They move the October public board meeting to November 4, 2026, at 5:30 pm Pacific in San Francisco, in room Waterfront E. The finance lead reports about $2.2 million in cash on hand, roughly 5.3 months of operating runway, and year-to-date net income near $790,000, with revenue ahead of budget.

Several governance issues come up. Accounts receivable write-offs, mostly small bank fees and sponsors that no longer exist, prompt a call for an approval process after one item exceeded a staff member's sign-off limit. Directors are asked to re-supply conflict-of-interest records that cannot be found. The website relaunch is delayed by a debate over going live without MFA or passkeys, after a director noted that weak passwords were still accepted. Policy reviews have stalled, so the board will rewrite the policy review policy itself, with status tracked on Monday.com. Legal advice on accepting project contributions from sanctioned countries leads to plans for click-through agreements at project creation. The project committee and education committee are to be notified that they risk dissolution if they stay inactive.

The closing reports cover a Black Hat and DEF CON trip, where a QR-code membership drive produced 353 scans and 115 new members. They also cover the Vienna event, which reportedly made about $320,000 profit against a budget of about $180,000 with 948 tickets sold. The meeting ends with a motion to adjourn that is approved.

talks.title: OWASP Finance Overview Presentation
talks.teaser: Walks through the foundation's June 2026 finances, showing cash reserves, revenue above budget and conference income driving results.
talks.summary:
This finance update for the OWASP Foundation reports the organization's position as of June 2026. Cash on hand is just under $2.5 million, which the presenter put at 6.6 months, and the current ratio is just over 9 to 1. Total net assets are just under $3.8 million, and cash has risen steadily since January to a twelve-month high.

Year-to-date total revenue is just over $3.4 million, against a budget of just over $2.6 million, and the same point last fiscal year showed about $2.6 million. Expenses are just under $2.15 million, below a budget of just under $2.6 million. The presenter expects trailing costs from the recent conference to ease next month. Net income is $1,269,000, compared with a budgeted $25,000 and $376,000 in the same period last year. Conference sponsorships make up 49% of revenue, and conference income overall, including registrations, training and sponsorships, makes up 73%. Conferences are also the largest expense at $854,000, followed by personnel and general and administrative costs.

The closing message is that revenue is beating expectations, costs are under budget and liquidity is solid, with a stronger second half expected. The team will keep monitoring receivables older than 90 days to make sure they can be collected.

talks.summary:
The recording opens an April 2026 OWASP Global Board meeting with roll call, antitrust and conflict-of-interest reminders, and approval of prior minutes. Leadership updates cover a finalized strategic plan, contracting for chapter ticket work, job postings with strong early applicant numbers, and postponement of AppSec Israel to October amid regional uncertainty, while rescheduling a virtual anniversary event so observers can participate.

Operations and finance dominate the middle. Staff cite supply-chain and endpoint-management incidents as reasons to refresh an IT security review and rotate website secrets before go-live, target penetration retesting within roughly two weeks, and document elections and awards procedures. Treasurer-style reporting highlights strong March cash and sponsorship pacing for the EU conference, while directors press for clearer budget context than raw year-to-date percentages. A new sponsorship lead outlines a 90-day plan for renewals, tiered materials, and sponsor outreach, and the policy review group urges a simpler full lifecycle governance rewrite.

Practitioners hear how a nonprofit security foundation balances volunteer chapters, vendor delivery, and compliance across EU VAT and insurance renewals. Takeaways include expecting phased website launch with auth testing and backup discipline, tighter guardrails on student chapters, faster chapter ticket communication, and board-led decisions before policy working groups edit community-facing rules.

talks.title: Securing Apps Without a Budget: Minimal Viable Security Strategies track 2
talks.teaser: Lays out low-cost security basics that small teams can apply to internet-facing apps before adding advanced measures.
talks.summary:
The talk introduces an application security poverty line, the minimum level of knowledge, investment and practice needed to protect software from common threats. The speaker calls the baseline minimal viable security (MVS) and aims it at small teams with no security budget or dedicated engineer. She argues that any internet-facing app that is not a static page should meet it at minimum.

The core checklist covers validating input and rejecting what fails, encoding output against cross-site scripting, using parameterized queries, choosing modern frameworks, and logging and monitoring. She advises buying tried-and-tested authentication rather than building it, keeping dependencies current, and outsourcing card payments so a processor carries PCI risk. Basic hygiene includes HTTPS everywhere, a free dynamic scanner run before going live, light threat modelling, and a security.txt file so people can report issues. Zero-day hunting, custom cryptography, complex role-based access control, obscurity and pentesting can wait.

Affordable developer training through OWASP chapters and free resources, security checks in code review, and a culture that rewards raising problems are covered. Signs an app has outgrown the baseline include incidents a team cannot handle, rapid growth or acquisitions. In the Q&A, she suggested vetting vendors' secure development processes and guiding AI coding tools with secure coding rules.

talks.title: Noise vs. Signal: The Central Paradox of LLMs in Threat Modeling track 2
talks.teaser: Argues LLM-only threat modeling yields inconsistent output and demos a repeatable NLP pipeline alternative.
talks.summary:
The speaker opens with feedback from about 100 AppSec leaders. They wanted an accurate model of the system built from many data sources, a way to surface surprising combinations of risks, alerts when earlier assumptions stop holding as systems change, and assurance that baseline controls exist before release. Many expected LLMs to deliver this, but running the same system description through an LLM-based threat generator produced different threats on different runs, so developers could not rely on the list or reproduce it.

The talk then looks at a published evaluation of an LLM threat-modeling co-pilot, where expert agreement with the model's threats varied sharply from system to system and many ratings were neutral. The speaker lists the risks of LLM-only threat modeling: missed threats, no confidence scores, automation bias that can erode threat modeling skills, weak reproducibility, and sensitivity to small wording changes. As an alternative, he demonstrates a deterministic pipeline. It parses text into entities and relationships, maps terms to a security ontology, builds a data flow graph with trust boundaries, and matches the result against CAPEC, CWE and STRIDE through a rule engine that checks compliance rules. In a live demo, a payment flow produced threats that changed when encryption and other controls were added to the graph.

The closing takeaway is a hybrid design: deterministic components handle the core analysis, while LLMs are used at the edges for brainstorming, summaries, rule drafting and the user interface. Unknown terms can be escalated to an LLM and labelled as such, so the output stays traceable. The speaker shares the demo code on GitHub as a starting point.

talks.title: Trust No One - Especially the Agents Building Zero Trust Through Machine Identity Track 2
talks.teaser: See how short-lived workload identities can constrain an AI agent’s access to business services.
talks.summary: The speaker explains how machine identities and AI agents challenge access controls built for human users, especially when agents rely on long-lived credentials across services. She describes a workload identity approach using SPIFFE and SPIRE to issue short-lived identities and credentials under resource-specific policies, then walks through a sales pipeline agent example. Attendees learn how this model can limit privileges, support revocation, and improve visibility into agent access.

talks.title: It’s Giving Insecure Vibes: Secure Coding Literacy for Vibe Coders Track 1
talks.teaser: Shows how AI-generated code hides common flaws and how vibe coders can spot and fix them through review and secure prompting.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at the security risks of vibe coding, where developers let an AI write most of an application with little review. The speaker argues that generated code can quickly hide problems such as exposed secrets, insecure defaults, missing authorization checks and unsanitized input. Examples included a login function with a to-do where verification should be, an MFA check that accepted a hard-coded value, MD5 password hashing, and a search feature that passed input straight into a query. Viral cases of exposed user data and an open database were used to show how fast prototypes can reach the public.

The middle of the session showed how to spot AI-written code. Signs include emojis in comments, overly tidy formatting, wordy print statements, leftover dead functions, imports that do not exist, and large commits that cannot be rolled back. A quiz had listeners find a command injection in a ping tool, a SQL query built from input despite a variable called clean, and a password echoed to logs. The speaker also covered supply-chain threats: typosquatted packages an assistant might suggest, proprietary code pasted into public models, and malicious editor extensions and agent skills.

The closing section focused on fixes. Developers should state security goals in prompts, design documents and instruction files, cite the OWASP Top 10, ask a fresh model session to review code skeptically, and run free scanners while feeding their output back to the assistant. For sensitive work, the speaker recommended offline local models, limiting autonomous trust modes to isolated environments, and keeping humans on login and data handling. The takeaway: AI should help experienced people work faster, not replace their review and judgement.

talks.title: 9125 Days of OWASP Did We Make Software Safer?
talks.teaser: An OWASP veteran asks whether 25 years of guidance improved software safety and what assurance must cover agents and AI-built code.
talks.summary:
Daniel Cuthbert opens with a blunt question tied to roughly 9,125 days of OWASP: did the movement make software safer? He is ambivalent. Vocabulary and awareness improved, yet severe flaws still appear constantly. He frames OWASP's story in acts, from pre-2001 web chaos through the 2001 launch, early projects such as the Top 10, development and testing guides, and Rogan Dawes's WebScarab proxy lineage.

He argues the terrain outran the map. Vibe coding lowers barriers but frontier models still ship SSRF, authorization gaps, and business-logic bugs; he demos a "secure" scanning API that fails on malicious URLs. Non-human identities already dwarf humans in Entro's 144-to-1 ratio, with most over-privileged. Wearables and agentic commerce shift risk onto people and devices. OpenClaw's rapid exposure and cascade failures illustrate bolt-on security after shipping.

He urges OWASP's next era to prioritize verification: machine-readable ASVS in CI/CD, standards for agents and delegation, wearables when the body is the surface, and metadata for AI-written code. Human engineers remain essential for threat thinking, ethics, and proving properties—not only generating code that works.

talks.title: OWASP Platinum Corporate Supporter - An Interview with Abraham Aranguren, of 7ASecurity
talks.teaser: Explains how a penetration testing firm runs audits, publishes open source reports and supports OWASP projects.
talks.summary:
Andrew van der Stock interviews Abraham Aranguren, managing director of 7ASecurity, about the firm's penetration tests and code audits across web, mobile, AI and cloud targets. Aranguren explains that each engagement opens a communication channel before testing starts, includes free fix verification, and concludes with an attestation letter. He also points to public reports the firm has published for open source projects, including Tor Project and Thunderbird Send.

The interview then covers OWTF, the Offensive Web Testing Framework, which began around 2008 as scripts automating Aranguren's OSCP preparation and later became an OWASP flagship project. The tool sorts its work by permission level, from passive reconnaissance that never contacts the target, to semi-passive requests, to active scanners run with client approval. Results appear in an interface where a tester verifies what is real. Aranguren recalls an authorization bypass he found by sending an unexpected HTTP method to a login page, which granted administrator access. He cautions that AI output must be validated by the professional who signs the report, and he stresses layered defenses and business logic testing.

For newcomers, he recommends contributing to an open source project in a chosen specialty, earning certifications, listening to security podcasts, giving lightning talks, joining OWASP chapter meetings and learning a programming language. He closes by noting that many widely used libraries, such as zlib, depend on unpaid maintainers, which makes formal audits valuable.

talks.title: OWASP Leaders Town Hall
talks.teaser: Foundation leaders outline Meetup exit, website migration, CRA readiness, policy reviews, and where chapter volunteers can plug in.
talks.summary:
The session opens with housekeeping on conduct and time, then walks chapter and project leaders through foundation priorities for the year. The board’s long-running strategy is being published in a usable form, an impact report awaits final financials, and the EU Cyber Resilience Act is framed as a driver for OWASP to act as an open-source steward with a vulnerability program and secure-coding policies volunteers can help draft. Term limits and flawed committee policy mean fresh volunteers are needed across chapter, project, and education committees, alongside a slate of policy reviews and a forthcoming AI use policy that requires disclosure and rejects low-quality automated submissions.

The core operational crisis is Meetup: new ownership is pressing for fees that would roughly triple the largest bill by 2027, from about fifty thousand dollars yearly toward one hundred sixty-five thousand, which the foundation rejects as incompatible with program spending. The plan is a unified chapter discovery path on the main site rather than a mix of paid Meetup groups, with Meetup kept temporarily until an MVP is ready, efforts to restore dozens of active-but-deleted groups, and careful handling of exported contact data for privacy law. GitHub Pages for chapters and events will move to the association site while top project sites can remain; infosec map and similar partners need updated meeting feeds.

The latter half focuses on the delayed Glue Up–based website: staff-heavy maintenance of the legacy multi-repo site, daily standups toward an MVP, penetration testing and a vulnerability disclosure program, XSS fixes, and scope-driven delays tied to the Meetup timeline. Leadership acknowledges December communication gaps as the main failure mode, discusses Eventbrite and Slack as future cost risks, and answers chapter questions on Luma, Compass, and social promotion while urging leaders to publish events centrally and join policy work.

talks.title: OWASP Global Board of Directors
talks.teaser: Board members approve governance policies, review finances and weigh website, GitHub security and anniversary plans.
talks.summary:
The December 2025 virtual meeting of the OWASP Foundation's global board opened with roll call, a conflict-of-interest reminder and approval of the previous month's minutes. The finance report showed cash falling by $203,000 to a balance of $1,754,875, with about 4.68 months of cash on hand. Directors agreed to roll over maturing certificates of deposit rather than withdraw them. A clean 2024 audit was noted, and the board discussed the concentration of risk across its two banks, though it did not propose opening more accounts.

Security and operations came next. After a recent run of attacks by a threat actor that steals credentials, the board decided to review its use of GitHub Actions and to protect the main branches of its repositories. The website rebuild was held back by a framework update and an independent penetration test, and the board asked for vendor patching commitments before launch. A proposal to add benefits for distinguished lifetime members was moved to the January meeting after community review. The board also adopted a board of directors policy, a matching bylaw change and an antitrust policy.

Looking ahead, the 25th anniversary program was outlined, with a leaders event in January, a set of chapter anniversary gatherings and a marketing plan for the first half of next year. That plan covers membership, corporate support and social media reach. Operations in Europe were being set up, with quarterly meetings expected for that entity. The meeting closed with thanks to departing directors and staff, and a special meeting was scheduled for January 5.

talks.title: Developer-Centric Threat Modeling: Embedding Security in Agile Workflows
talks.teaser: Shows developers a rapid, template-driven threat modeling method that scopes work to single components.
talks.summary:
The session presents RATM, a rapid threat modeling methodology for developers that reduces reliance on security experts. The speakers argue that traditional threat modeling, which often covers a whole application and needs specialist input, is resource intensive and yields vague results. Their approach narrows scope to individual components, such as an authentication service or a payment flow, so the owning team can model it.

The core enabler is the threat template: a predefined set of up to 20 threats, each with a description, default severity and controls. Templates cover implementation, deployment environment, compliance standards such as PCI DSS, and organizational priorities. In a Java banking transfer app on AWS, a developer, a cloud engineer and a risk owner each applied their own template after drawing trust boundaries, then marked each threat mitigated, unmitigated or accepted.

For rollout, the speakers covered three cases: a small Kanban team using spreadsheets, a mid-sized Scrum organization with a central cyber team tailoring templates, and a large regulated firm using SAFe. Developers build the models while security teams review them. Automation and generative AI could speed up diagram drawing and control mapping.

talks.title: Post-Quantum Threats in Real Code: Finding and Fixing Cryptographic Risk at Scale
talks.teaser: Shows how type-aware recipes and cross-repository taint analysis can locate hard-coded cryptography across massive banking codebases.
talks.summary:
Financial institutions need to find cryptographic patterns in their source code, such as hard-coded algorithms, keys, certificates and provider names, that would have to change before a post-quantum migration. The talk explains why this is hard at scale. A generic method name like getInstance appears on hundreds of distinct receiver types across open source projects, so plain text or syntax matching produces too many false positives. One banking customer alone has about 500 million lines of code under management.

The speaker's approach builds on OpenRewrite, which represents code as a lossless semantic tree with type attribution. That lets a recipe confirm which class a call really belongs to and whether a method is deprecated, even when the annotation sits several interfaces up. Recipes can emit data tables that feed later runs, which supports intra-file and then cross-file taint analysis. Multi-stage taint pipelines let each stage record the taint types it emits, and precomputed method summaries cover binary dependencies without source. Examples included a deprecated-method search across about 200 repositories and a large migration recipe to Spring Boot 3.4 with roughly 3,000 steps.

Questions from the audience turned to the social side of change. Automated pull requests from a central team are often rejected, so the speaker described unit tests with before-and-after cases and a progressive rollout that grows safer as teams find new edge cases. The main takeaway is to map the blast radius first, and to consider centralising cryptographic choices in shared libraries so future algorithm changes are cheaper.

talks.title: Towards the next generation OWASP CRS ruleset language
talks.teaser: Presents CRS Lang, a proposed YAML-based replacement for SecLang WAF rules, with a parser and translator tool.
talks.summary:
The talk introduces a proposed successor to SecLang, the rule language behind the OWASP Core Rule Set (CRS), a widely used open-source web application firewall ruleset of roughly 400 rules. The speakers explain why the current syntax is a problem: rules are tied to the behaviour of specific engines such as ModSecurity and Coraza, they are hard for newcomers to read, and they cannot easily be reused or templated. Logic is also hard to follow, since set actions in one rule can change the variables that a chained rule inspects, and AND and OR conditions are awkward to express.

The proposed language, called CRS Lang, is written in YAML with a clear split between metadata, conditions and actions. Conditions become an ordered list, and disruptive and non-disruptive actions are grouped separately. The team built a parser with ANTLR that reads SecLang versions 2 and 3, offered in Go and Python, along with a translator that converts in both directions. Comments that explain how a rule works are carried over into the new format, and the generated output is checked with the existing CRS validation tools.

A live demo converted a sample rule into the new format and regenerated SecLang output that matched the original behaviour. Side effects, templating and adoption by the engines remain open questions. The speakers asked the community for feedback on the syntax and suggested that a YAML schema could bring editor autocompletion and validation. The main takeaway is that the project is seeking input on the design before it moves further.

talks.title: Chinese PRC shenanigans in the npm mirror ecosystem
talks.teaser: Shows how some Chinese npm mirrors keep serving malicious packages that npm has already removed, and how to retrieve them.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at how npm, the largest JavaScript package registry, removes malicious packages, and how several of its mirrors in China handle those removals differently. The speaker, an independent researcher who focuses on npm malware, explains that npm now usually removes reported packages within about 48 hours, compared with a historical average of 29 days. He also describes quiet removals, where npm replaces every version of a package with a placeholder, and attackers who delete their own packages to limit analysis.

The core finding is that some Chinese mirrors keep serving packages that npm has already deleted. One mirror kept serving malicious versions for days, weeks or sometimes months after removal. Two others ignored deletion events entirely, and two more returned not-found responses, which the speaker links to the placeholder behaviour. He used this gap to collect removed malware samples, analysed them to write detection rules, and released an open-source npm tool, unddelete, which he says works roughly 60 to 70 percent of the time. He also reports that default Artifactory instances and corporate mirrors can keep deleted packages, and that his own canary packages were hit weeks after deletion.

The speaker says the mirror behaviour is too consistent to be accidental and suggests government involvement is possible, though he cannot prove it. For practitioners, the takeaway is that deleted npm packages may persist in mirrors and internal repositories, so removal from the public registry is not the end of the exposure. He points to a free database, opensourcemalware.com, for tracking malicious package components.

Some require one bad click by the victim, others work with no user interaction – 0click attacks.

talks.title: One Cluster to Rule Them All: Pentesting Multi-Tenant Kubernetes Clusters
talks.teaser: Shows how a compromised tenant developer can probe a shared Kubernetes cluster for secrets and exposed services.
talks.summary:
This talk examines how much isolation a shared, multi-tenant Kubernetes cluster actually gives development teams. The speaker argues that compliance and audit tools reporting a cluster as healthy can miss real exposure, and that the reliable check is to attack it from the view of a compromised tenant. Namespaces and role-based access control form the base, while a tenancy plugin and a policy engine let teams self-serve without running privileged containers.

The demos start from a simulated developer account in one tenant. Listing with the get-all command shows only a fraction of what exists because custom resources are missed, so the speaker dumps everything to offline files and flags a base64-encoded secret that was hardcoded in a manifest. The attacker identity then tries to create service account tokens, copy files from pods and exec into workloads. One unprotected namespace yielded tokens that could enable lateral movement. A sweep over every resource tests read and modify rights. For networking, a pod whose port was never declared still served a web service, so scanning must cover the full port range. Pod IPs were gathered and scanned from inside the cluster and correlated to the services behind them.

The talk closes by noting that pod-to-pod traffic is unrestricted by default unless network policies are added, and that cloud network plugins can let pods reach other VPC resources. A tenant could also hijack another team's ingress route. Practitioners should test from a tenant's perspective, enforce network policies and policy agents, and not rely on audit output alone.

talks.title: The Most Common AppSec Failures in Fortune 500 Companies and Beyond
talks.teaser: Five recurring mistakes from Fortune 500 assessments, with practical fixes for risk, threat modeling, requirements, tools, and metrics.
talks.summary:
Large organizations often ramp up application security after an incident, then slip back into old habits. The presenter describes lessons from more than forty in-depth paired assessments, overwhelmingly at Fortune 500 scale, built around long stakeholder interviews and follow-up improvement cycles. The talk is framed as five ways organizations undermine their own programs, with a sixth theme around isolating security teams left out for time.

The first failure is treating every application as equally mission critical instead of building a shared risk picture from executives through development and operations. Threat modeling goes wrong when one hero produces a PDF, when external teams do architecture review masquerading as threat modeling, or when tools and AI replace collaborative practice before basics exist. Teams also confuse training, pentest findings, or one-off SSO work with systematic security requirements; the speaker ties requirements to confidentiality, integrity, and availability expectations and points to ASVS as a starting set in sprint planning. Tool-centric programs create false comfort, especially where dependency data leans on CVE and CVSS signals that research shows are noisy or inconsistent. Metrics fail when dashboards lead instead of organizational goals; the goal–question–metric approach is offered as a corrective, with an example around high-risk production fix time.

Practical guidance includes simple risk questionnaires, time-boxed collaborative threat sessions whose outputs live in issue trackers, labeled security requirements and threat items, processes before scanners with owned configurations, and metrics chosen only after goals and questions are clear.

talks.title: Breaking the Black Box - Using the OWASP Threat Model Library to End Security via Obscurity
talks.teaser: Argues for publishing sanitized threat models and shows how to contribute one to the OWASP Threat Model Library.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that organisations should publish their threat models rather than keep them secret. The speaker points to European rules such as NIS2, the Cyber Resilience Act and DORA, which emphasise incident disclosure, transparency and risk assessment. A show of hands suggested many attendees already build threat models, and several would consider publishing them.

The speaker lists benefits including trust with customers and regulators, crowdsourced hardening from peer feedback, career portfolios and audit-ready evidence. Concerns such as handing attackers a map, exposing architecture to competitors, legal issues, keeping models current and customers misreading them are acknowledged. Suggested mitigations are a narrow scope, sanitising sensitive detail, implementing the main controls first, involving legal, and using automation or AI tooling.

The speaker demonstrated a pull request adding an internal threat model for a Forge app integration in Jira, which initially failed the schema check. Drafting tools mentioned included AI coding assistants, Threat Dragon for data-flow visualisation and Mermaid charts. In the Q&A, questions covered anonymous submission, peer review as the planned quality control, and checking currency through the version and publication date in the schema. The closing message was to start small, publish, and then iterate.

talks.title: OWASP AIBOM: Pioneering AI Transparency Through Community-Driven Standards
talks.teaser: Introduces the OWASP AI Bill of Materials project, its ten workstreams, and how volunteers can help shape AI transparency standards.
talks.summary:
The talk introduces the OWASP AI Bill of Materials project, a young, volunteer-driven effort that extends software bill of materials thinking to AI systems. The speaker explains that regulations increasingly ask how AI-enabled applications were built, including which datasets and models they use, and that the project aims to give organizations practical guidance on what to record and what to do first when a foundation model is involved in a breach.

The project is organized into ten work streams. Prerequisites cover a gap analysis of existing SBOM standards and the identification of AI components. A formats stream looks at CycloneDX and SPDX, while a tooling stream covers open-source and commercial tools and conversion between formats. Governance work considers where AI bills of materials should be stored, how a recipient can verify who signed them, and the legal implications of sharing them. Other streams focus on adoption guidance, policy engagement, and collaboration with other foundations, universities and companies.

Near the end, the speaker described the timeline, with the aim of reaching the main goals by February or March of the following year, and reported around 72 direct and indirect contributors. Audience members with compliance backgrounds described difficulties gathering evidence, especially at small businesses, and one noted the need for AI-specific control detail comparable to a CIS benchmark. The session closed with ways to join: a weekly recorded call, a Slack channel, a project page and a sign-up form.

talks.title: OWASP DefectDojo
talks.teaser: Explains how DefectDojo merges scanner results into one deduplicated findings list, and where the OWASP project goes next.
talks.summary:
The talk introduces DefectDojo, an OWASP project, and the vulnerability management problem it was built to address. The speaker helped create it while running product security at Rackspace, where many teams used different scanners and produced different output. Spreadsheets could not keep up with that volume, so the project set out to collect results in one central place. It imports output from 206 supported scanners, and a generic importer accepts CSV or JSON from anything else. A REST API lets teams automate the work instead of doing it by hand.

The middle of the talk covers the features that set the platform apart. Deduplication removes repeated results within one tool or across several, and finding groups let related issues, such as several weaknesses in one TLS configuration, become a single ticket. Reimporting a recurring scan lets DefectDojo close findings that disappear and reopen ones that return, keeping their history. A bidirectional Jira integration syncs status, comments and tags. The speaker suggests running a candidate scanner through DefectDojo to test it against an environment, which also makes it easier to change vendors later without reworking downstream workflows.

The closing section covers the project's growth and direction. Figures cited include about 38 million downloads, more than 400 contributors and over 10,000 pull requests and issues. DefectDojo Pro is a commercial offering layered on the open-source code, and its revenue now funds full-time maintainers, community support and documentation work. Planned items include a revamped community site, better docs, dark mode, contributor rewards and a UI refresh for the open-source edition.

talks.title: Building a Static Analyzer from Scratch
talks.teaser: Covers design principles for security scanners, using a GitHub Actions analyzer as a case study in usability.
talks.summary:
The speaker presents opinions drawn from years of building and deploying static analysis tools for coworkers, rather than a tutorial. Static analysis here means reasoning about code without running it, such as asking which calls reach a function or whether user input flows into a value. GitHub Actions is the focus because its workflow files branch little and are comparatively easy to reason about. Two common flaws are shown: pull request text expanded into a shell command, and checking out a pull request's code and running its tests alongside secrets.

Principles are tied to examples. A Ruby linter rule that followed return values found more bugs but also more false positives, so the speaker removed the configuration option and tuned the algorithm instead. ShellCheck is praised for pinpointing the line and giving a concrete fix, and RuboCop for letting teams adopt new rules gradually via namespaces and severity thresholds. The speaker also favors a pattern-matching language over raw syntax tree code, and normalizing YAML so rule authors need less format knowledge.

The closing points cover readable code and tests, being open about why each detection exists and how noisy it may be, and keeping a corpus of vulnerable samples to test against. In questions, the speaker argues that rule-based tools suit open-ended inputs, that structured output helps AI consumers, and that AI and classic analysis should be combined rather than one replacing the other. The takeaway: moving from good to great depends more on usability and design than on technical capability.

talks.title: In GitHub We Trust: 10 Ways You Could Get Pwned
talks.teaser: Shows how GitHub-referenced dependencies, build files and CI actions can silently compromise pipelines, and how to pin them.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that teams who scan their application dependencies often ignore open source pulled into the rest of the software development lifecycle straight from GitHub. The presenters say GitHub hosts a far larger attack surface than public package registries, and that references to branches, tags or other mutable pointers let upstream code change without anyone noticing. They walk through ten routes to compromise. These include npm, pip and Maven dependencies that point at a GitHub branch, a Go module case where a malicious version stayed cached in the module proxy after the author cleaned up the repository, and Dockerfiles that clone repositories at build time.

The later cases cover Helm charts, where the packaged archive can differ from the repository the team reviewed; configuration and observability tools such as Ansible, SaltStack, Logstash and Grafana that can load code from GitHub; repository webhooks; GitHub Actions compromised through re-pointed version tags; git submodules; Terraform modules; and Gradle scripts that run during a build. Each demonstration showed data being exfiltrated while the application still appeared to work normally. The speakers also noted that install-time hooks can execute code before the package is ever run.

For mitigation, the presenters recommend pinning GitHub references to a full commit SHA and scanning those fixed versions, including transitive dependencies. They suggest extending the SBOM to list GitHub references and SDLC tooling, keeping an approved set of vetted sources in an internal registry, and involving security teams during planning. In the Q&A they acknowledged that pinning does not reach every deeper dependency, and that standard composition-analysis tools do not fully cover this case.

talks.title: Threat Modeling Developer Behaviour: The Psychology of Bad Code
talks.teaser: Explains how cognitive biases and incentives drive insecure developer habits, and how to nudge teams toward secure code.
talks.summary:
Tanya Jenko argues that insecure code often comes from predictable human behaviour rather than a lack of knowledge. Drawing on behavioural economics, she treats bad developer habits as patterns that can be designed around, without blaming individuals. She walks through ten common insecure behaviours, including vibe coding, copying snippets from forums, rushing near deadlines, skipping error handling and documentation, chasing new technology, and faking code review, and links each one to a cognitive bias or heuristic.

For each pattern, the proposed fixes work at several levels. Secure defaults, such as an ORM that refuses inline query language or a shared template that validates input, remove the need for willpower. Checks built into the SDLC, IDE plugins, pre-commit hooks and CI/CD gates that block critical findings make secure choices routine. On the training side, she recommends short, recurring sessions, social learning such as pairing a senior developer with someone who made a mistake, and positive feedback for wanted behaviour. She also suggests measuring behaviour change rather than course completion.

She ends with three shifts: from secure intentions to secure defaults, from annual training to ongoing cultural reinforcement, and from blaming individuals to redesigning the environment. Practical next steps include choosing one secure default to implement, adding a behavioural risk to the next threat model, and tracking how behaviour changes over time.

talks.title: SBOMs in the Real World: Practical Guidance for Managing Three Common SBOM Scenarios
talks.teaser: Walks through three real-world SBOM scenarios: generation, aggregation for risk prioritization, and supplier exchange.
talks.summary:
The talk covers how organizations can get more out of software bills of materials (SBOMs) once they can generate them reliably. It organizes the discussion around three scenarios that build on each other: regular generation, aggregation and centralization, and exchange with suppliers and customers. The speaker recommends producing an SBOM right after the build and again before deployment, since those reflect the artifact that customers actually receive.

For aggregation, the speaker explains that a central view lets teams quickly find which products are affected when a malicious package surfaces. One example describes a financial services customer with about 10,000 applications built on a shared Spring-based SDK, where what looked like 10,000 vulnerabilities came down to a single upgrade. Prioritization questions cover asset criticality, whether a vulnerability is exploitable in context, and whether a safe fix exists. The main obstacle raised is unique component identification, since distribution-specific Linux packages can carry different vulnerability data, so purl or CPE identifiers are preferred over loose matching.

For exchange, the speaker says few organizations have reached this stage yet. Supplier workflows involve checking incoming SBOMs against your own policies, asking for updated VEX statements when new vulnerabilities appear, and pinning each SBOM to a specific release. The talk closes by urging teams to centralize around unique identifiers, move SBOM sharing away from email, and recognize that license risk can become a security risk.

talks.title: OWASP Global Board of Directors
talks.teaser: Records the OWASP board's November 2025 meeting, covering finances, a tabled election policy and a proposed audit committee.
talks.summary:
The November 2025 OWASP Global Board meeting opened with roll call, a conflict-of-interest check and a vote to add two motions to the agenda. The board approved October's minutes, then heard management reports. The annual US tax filing was submitted on time and accepted, and the audit was completed with a clean opinion. The outside finance provider summarised October results, noting conference income ahead of budget but corporate supporter renewals behind.

The marketing lead introduced three near-term projects: a Giving Tuesday campaign, a marketing strategy due in December, and a 2025 annual report planned for January. A proposed marketing working group was tabled. The 2026 budget draft remained incomplete while staff entered event figures, with approval targeted for January. Members also questioned high food and beverage costs at conferences and whether sponsors could fund meals.

A new board of directors policy was tabled until December after late feedback. Points under review included antitrust wording, a 12-month cooling-off period for former staff, code-of-conduct eligibility checked against a compliance list, and background checks limited by local law. A proposed board audit and risk committee drew broad support, pending a name and charter. The meeting closed by moving into executive session.

talks.title: OWASP Top 10 for LLMs
talks.teaser: Explains OWASP's LLM top risks, focusing on prompt injection and excessive agency, with app architecture and simple mitigations.
talks.summary:
The speaker frames the talk as a look at three OWASP top 10 risks for LLM applications, after sketching how these apps are built. Early designs used a front end, application code and a vector database of embedded proprietary data. Newer agentic designs add a message bus, control plane and agents that call tools through model context protocol servers.

Prompt injection is treated as the LLM version of SQL injection, where user input concatenated into a prompt can override intended instructions. Two CVEs in open-source libraries reportedly allowed remote code execution through crafted prompts. Suggested defenses include separating system instructions from user input, sanitizing inputs and using filtering libraries together. For sensitive information disclosure, unrestricted retrieval can return any embedded record, so user roles should be passed down to the vector store, with output filtering, anonymization and data minimization.

Excessive agency appears in an attack idea described in published research, where hidden unprintable characters in AI coding rule files alter model behavior unseen by developers. A local setup where a model runs any terminal command shows the same risk. Mitigations include an allowed-command list, sandboxed execution and avoiding broad permissions. The speaker closes by noting that AI components lack the community reputation earlier open-source tools built, and asks for feedback.

talks.title: API Fuzzing in the SSDLC Problems and Possible Solutions
talks.teaser: Explains how a bank's AppSec team built an automated API fuzzer for thousands of teams, covering schema discovery, auth, and triage.
talks.summary:
The speaker, an application security engineer at a large European bank, explains why API fuzzing matters for thousands of development teams on short release cycles. Many APIs go untested because teams rely on unit tests, pentests or bug bounties, and API schemas are often missing or outdated. The team first tried several open-source fuzzers, found they lacked the features they needed, and decided to build an in-house tool.

The architecture uses containerised workers behind a manager that validates requests and feeds a message queue, with object storage holding large result sets. When no OpenAPI schema exists, the tool scans source code for route definitions and can use an internally hosted language model to build a schema for legacy systems. Authentication is limited to mutual TLS or tokens supplied by the owning team. Modules test for injection, denial of service, broken access control, race conditions and SSRF through a callback address.

To keep noise down, the team ignores most 400 and 404 responses, treats server errors as candidate findings, and groups results by endpoint with a curl command for reproduction. Firewalls, separate network zones and blocking by a blue team created practical obstacles. The talk concludes that fuzzing works best inside CI/CD with incremental scans of changed code, with results reported per release in an application security management platform.

talks.title: Building Resilient Applications with Effective Threat Modeling
talks.teaser: Covers why threat modeling often fails in organizations and how to make it a continuous, cross-team practice.
talks.summary:
The speakers frame application resilience as an application's ability to adapt and recover from hardware or software failures and cyber attacks. They argue that smaller organizations without large budgets still need practical ways to get there, and they point to a 2024 survey in which 45% of organizations did not perform threat modeling consistently.

The talk breaks threat modeling into identifying, assessing, mitigating and validating threats, then into five steps: setting objectives, visualizing the architecture with data flow diagrams, identifying threats with frameworks such as STRIDE and MITRE ATT&CK, mitigating by ranking threats and adding controls, and validating those controls after deployment. The presenters stress that applying one framework consistently matters more than choosing the perfect one. They then describe five common pitfalls: modeling only once as a single event, relying on known threats and checklists, keeping security in a silo, treating every finding as critical, and leaving findings in a spreadsheet without owners or deadlines.

For each pitfall they suggest a fix: revisit models throughout the development lifecycle, think like an attacker instead of following the book, bring in developers, architects and business stakeholders, prioritize by likelihood and impact, and track findings with tickets, owners and deadlines. In the Q&A, they suggested existing frameworks can still apply to AI risks such as tampered training data, and advised starting with one threat and widening coverage over time. The closing message is a shift in mindset: threat modeling is an ongoing strategy, not a checkbox.

talks.title: Day In the Life Of Supply Chain Security Researcher
talks.teaser: Walks through how two researchers turn open source vulnerability advisories into reachable detection rules for a code scanner.
talks.summary:
The talk follows two supply chain security researchers through their daily work of converting open source vulnerability advisories into rules for a code scanner. They explain the three rule types: automated version checks, reviewed upgrade-only rules, and reachable rules that search code for the vulnerable function. Because new CVEs arrive daily, they prioritize by ecosystem coverage, customer usage, CVSS severity, and EPSS exploitation likelihood.

Advisory quality varies widely. A well-written lodash advisory lists the affected functions, so a rule can be drafted in minutes. A sparse Apache Commons Compress advisory only gives a patch version, so the researchers compare the 1.25 and 1.26 releases, work through a diff of roughly 600 commits, and search for fix commits to find the vulnerable path. For a Python download function in a parallel library, they map the call graph from the affected function up through its callers, then test the draft rule against sample code for both false positives and false negatives.

After shipping, they measure rules using scan data from users who opted in. For the lodash rule, about 185,000 findings were reported, with only around 80,000 reachable, so roughly 40% of affected projects call the vulnerable function. They also describe BRAT, an internal LLM tool that drafts missing proof-of-concept code, which they still review manually. The takeaway is that a data-driven approach focused on real call sites keeps the backlog manageable, and they invite ideas on measuring rule effectiveness.

talks.title: Analyzing Zero Trust Architecture in the Age of Agentic GenAI
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding Analyzing Zero Trust Architecture in the Age of Agentic GenAI.
talks.summary: Vinit Narjala, Application Security Engineer at AWS, presents a framework for securing autonomous AI agents using zero trust principles. He distinguishes agentic AI from traditional LLMs by highlighting agents' planning, reasoning, memory (short and long-term), tool integration, and autonomous action capabilities—creating significantly larger attack surfaces. Narjala identifies four new threat domains beyond traditional appsec: cognitive security (reasoning hijacking, goal manipulation), execution integrity (tool misuse, code execution risks), identity coherence (authentication/authorization across agent lifecycles), and governance complexity (multi-agent delegation chains). He maps 15 OWASP agentic AI threats into the ATFAA (Advanced Framework for Autonomous Agents) framework. The core defense strategy is ATBMF (Adaptive Trust Boundary Management Framework), a three-pillar approach: (1) Multi-dimensional Monitoring and Observability—capturing action-intent correlation, data access patterns, resource utilization, and communication patterns via deterministic hooks into agent workflows; (2) Dynamic Policy Enforcement—using graduated access (full/limited/read-only/deny), just-in-time privileges, automatic credential revocation, and contextual reauthentication to adjust trust boundaries in real-time based on risk scores; (3) Self-Healing Procedures—network isolation, quarantining, graceful degradation, and forensic state preservation. Narjala demonstrates an AWS implementation with API Gateway and Lambda fronting agents, where Lambda enforces policies before requests reach agents and dynamically attaches scoped IAM policies based on intent and risk profile. Real-world vulnerabilities cited include Outlook Copilot exfiltrating Slack tokens via prompt injection, Morse code bypassing guardrails, and steganographic image injection. The framework balances developer velocity with security by enabling controlled innovation in sandboxed environments rather than blocking adoption. Key mitigations include avoiding code execution access unless necessary, network isolating per-user interactions, using VMs for isolation, never passing credentials to agents, limiting input prompts to predefined options (like SQL stored procedures), and maintaining deterministic security decisions independent of model outputs. Narjala emphasizes that prompt injection is a built-in feature, not a bug, making architectural controls and guardrails paramount. The three core takeaways: operationalize AI with zero trust, model the agent itself (not just the application), and enable developers while keeping security satisfied.

talks.title: OWASP Global Board of Directors Meeting
talks.teaser: Covers the OWASP Foundation board's June 2025 meeting: finances, audit prep, bylaw proposals and marketing hiring.
talks.summary:
The chair opened the June 2025 general board meeting, confirmed the agenda by a vote that kept a marketing item, and approved the May minutes after a dispute over whether the earlier electronic vote record had been published. A director abstained. The staff update then covered several workstreams: a new EU entity still waiting on Belgian approval before it can open bank accounts, a website redesign being reviewed as Figma wireframes, planning for the 25th anniversary, and two open roles, one of which was covered on an acting basis.

Finance and operations took most of the remaining time. The 2024 audit fieldwork was set to start on July 7, with a draft targeted for the end of September and the 990 due on November 15. Around $295,000 of income remained uncategorised at the end of May, $187,000 of it from the Glue Up event and membership platform, which made event-level profit and loss statements hard to produce. Staff also described a chapter and membership ticket backlog that would need cover during summer leave, and a review of subscriptions and software seats to cancel unused platforms. A proposal to extend board terms from two years to four drew objections about burnout and commitment. The board agreed that the idea needed more justification and a check against Delaware nonprofit rules, and that the election bylaw changes could not land before the August deadline.

The meeting closed with a working group for the 25th anniversary, a request for the chapter committee to bring its charter back for a vote in July, and a marketing hire targeted for the end of July. The main takeaway for other nonprofits is to align payment platform categories with accounting codes early, before event revenue becomes impossible to attribute. The next general board meeting was set for July 22, 2025.

talks.title: OWASP Global Board of Directors Meeting
talks.teaser: Records the OWASP board's May 2025 meeting, covering votes on policies, the Vienna conference, finances and the EU entity.
talks.summary:
This recording covers the OWASP global board meeting held in May 2025. Directors approved a contract for Vienna as the host venue for the European conference from 2026 to 2028, at 157K per year, and passed motions creating working groups, adopting a working group policy, and approving a privacy policy and a travel policy.

Finance and operations updates were given by the executive director and a charity CFO. Cash was reported at about 2.3 million after registration and training revenue rose, and year-to-date net income was put at 816,000. About 80,000 in receivables more than 90 days old was collected. Legal advice on US work authorization for trainers was flagged as a constraint on who can teach at US events, and the board discussed promoting the European conference as an international option for attendees worried about crossing the border.

The board also covered the planned EU entity, which will handle more contracts and may apply for EU grants, along with the certification program's curriculum and exam question bank work and a planned marketing hire tied to a new outreach working group. The meeting shows how the foundation is setting up its governance, budget and certification plans.

talks.title: OWASP Corporate Supporter Spotlight - root.io
talks.teaser: A sponsor interview covering a container-patching startup's origins, advice for founders, and how it supports OWASP projects.
talks.summary:
OWASP's executive director hosts a conversation with John Amal, who describes the company he co-founded to fix vulnerabilities in container images. He traces its origin to repeated difficulty managing vulnerabilities in products he ran at Cisco, which led him to build a company focused on that problem.

The guest explains that the platform patches container images using compatible upgrades and backported fixes for Debian, Ubuntu, Alpine and Python packages, with an agentic system producing new patches. Results are shared as CycloneDX VEX statements and SBOMs, and the company also uses Dependency-Track to track its software supply chain. On startups, his advice covers choosing co-founders who complement each other, testing the idea and selling from the first day, and finding mentors and early customers who can vouch for the product. The discussion also covers how OWASP might support project leaders who spin out companies, with a premium version keeping the open-source project alive.

Near the end, the guest argues that open-source maintainers lack incentives to vet packages, and that companies building on open source should give back. He closes by offering OWASP and Dependency-Track users free access to zero-vulnerability Dependency-Track container images through his platform, with a follow-up planned.

talks.title: 202011 November 2020 Global Board Meeting
talks.teaser: Records an OWASP Foundation board meeting covering finances, a virtual events vote, an Australia 2021 proposal and policy reform.
talks.summary:
The November 2020 global board meeting of the OWASP Foundation opened with approval of earlier minutes and a review of organizational KPIs. Membership grew by about 145 people through the virtual conference, while website visitors declined and the cheat sheets became one of the most popular parts of the site. The election drew just over 20% of membership votes, and the executive director outlined a staff review of policies against actual procedures.

The financial update covered the year to date through October. Net income was described as on track or somewhat better than forecast, and cash stood at about 1.36 million dollars, roughly 13 months of reserve. Board members asked about plans to move banking to a Money Corp account, which would avoid currency conversion fees, and about how European sponsorship and donation deductions would work. The board then passed an electronic vote approving a virtual events strategy with a budget of 41,500, six to one.

The largest item was a proposal to run a global AppSec event in Australia in 2021, with projected income of 290,000 and expenses of 234,000. A board member pointed out that the stated net profit should be about 56,000, not 55,000. Discussion covered border uncertainty, the need for an Australian entity to apply for a government grant closing 30 November, and venue and force majeure terms. The motion was approved, and the meeting closed with discussion of expense reform, ending chapter balances and a grants-based funding model.

talks.summary:
### Overview
The OWASP July 2020 Global Board of Directors meeting addressed critical operational, financial, and governance matters facing the organization amid the COVID-19 pandemic. Key items discussed included the approval of meeting minutes, reviews of executive director and finance reports, the creation of an Education and Training Committee, the status of regional and global conferences transitioning to virtual formats, election timelines, and proposed bylaw amendments regarding board member term limits and eligibility.

### Key Topics
- **Financial Status & Cash Reserves**: Tom presented the financial update showing revenues through June were roughly $26,000 ahead of forecast, partially because conference income cushioned deficits in memberships and donations. Total net deficit stood at approximately $112,000 to $166,500 year-to-date. Cash on hand was around $1.465 million at the end of June, projected to decline to around $1 million by year-end. A central concern discussed was OWASP's reliance on conferences as an "events company" and assessing whether the foundation would have a sufficient cash runway into 2021 if physical conferences remain halted.
- **Executive Director Report & External Affiliations**: Andrew van der Stock provided updates on membership growth (+61 net), website traffic (554k visitors), and declining service desk tickets. He announced policy community reviews, the move to fully virtual events, and that OWASP joined the Linux Foundation and the Open Source Security Foundation (OpenSSF), with board member Sherif Mansour appointed to the OpenSSF board.
- **Education Committee Approval**: Grant sponsored a motion to formally approve the establishment of the Education and Training Committee following the Committee 2.0 structure, led by community members Adrian and John. The motion passed unanimously (7–0).
- **Virtual vs. Regional Events Strategy**: The board evaluated how to address cancellations of major regional conferences (such as AppSec California and AppSec Cali/Dublin concerns). Discussion centered on providing chapters with virtual event tooling (e.g., StreamYard) and guidance rather than the central foundation taking over regional conferences, avoiding brand dilution and staff burnout.
- **Bylaw Amendments on Board Eligibility & Term Limits**: Significant debate occurred regarding compliance committee recommendations to clarify board term limits. Specifically, discussions focused on whether filling a partial vacancy should count as a full term or count toward term limits, how to measure time served (e.g., splitting by one year or setting a five-year cap), and the ethics of altering eligibility rules immediately prior to the upcoming election cycle when it could directly impact sitting board members. The topic was deferred for further public discussion and separated into discrete votes.

talks.title: 202005 May 2020 Global Board Meeting
talks.teaser: Walks through an OWASP Foundation board meeting covering finances, pandemic-era events, membership and governance motions.
talks.summary:
The board opened by approving the April meeting minutes, then received reports on key performance indicators, finances and executive operations. Membership rose the previous month, website traffic was down about 6% year on year, and cash on hand was roughly $1.4 million. Year-to-date the organisation was about $35,000 in deficit, well inside a budgeted loss of about $213,000, while chapter balances of roughly $888,000 kept growing. Virtual events were described as profitable, with about $165,000 in revenue.

Discussion then moved to events and staffing. The San Francisco event faced a registration launch targeted for June and a go or no-go decision at the July meeting, and the board discussed how regional conferences in Europe and North America would be spread through the year. Defcon and Black Hat had been cancelled, and the board debated whether OWASP should join the virtual village events run by others. A marketing plan was presented as a short abstract, and a member asked for more emphasis on promoting the open-source projects. A request for a detailed events project plan led to a commitment to share a revised task sheet once it was scrubbed for completeness.

Three motions were on the table and all were tabled. A proposal to buy board training and assessment services from an outside provider was set aside because members wanted fuller information on cost and benefits, with a suggestion to compare alternatives first. A motion restricting in-person chapter meetings during the pandemic was tabled so its wording on local legal rules and reasonable chapter expenses could be redrafted and voted on by email. A motion granting one-year honorary memberships to four applicants was also tabled, with the membership committee asked to define criteria and staff to collect the rationale from each applicant. Budget amendments were deferred to the next meeting.

talks.title: 202004 April 2020 Global Board Meeting
talks.teaser: The board weighs COVID-19 fallout on events, finances and the website, and adopts a revised 2020 budget.
talks.summary:
This recorded board meeting from April 2020 looks at how the COVID-19 lockdown is affecting the foundation. Directors approved the previous month's minutes, then heard an operations report showing website traffic dipping as the lockdown began. Membership figures rose because of free memberships given to a California event's attendees. Staff also described a payroll protection loan application, the first virtual event series, and a sponsorship pipeline that had shrunk sharply since March.

The finance update showed revenue on budget and expenses well under budget through March, with a year-over-year comparison planned. A discussion of transfer fees on reimbursements paid through the European entity led to talk of alternative payment methods. The board then approved signing venue agreements for a North American event in 2021 and a European event in 2022. Cancelling the 2020 San Francisco venue would have cost roughly $120,000, so a negotiated deal cut the penalty to $32,000 with a matching credit toward 2021.

The board adopted a revised 2020 budget, Model Z, with caps on travel, chapter spending and discretionary costs, plus a moratorium on new event contracts. A go or no-go decision on San Francisco is due by late July. Directors also asked staff for project plans for major events and a marketing plan, and discussed a shared events calendar. The main lesson is that event-dependent income left the foundation exposed, so it needs diversification and written plans.

talks.title: 20201116 November 2021 Events Special Board Meeting
talks.teaser: Board members weigh OWASP's 2021 event options, venue contracts and sponsor revenue as the pandemic disrupts conference plans.
talks.summary:
The board met to decide how the OWASP Foundation should approach its events in 2021 while pandemic restrictions were still in place. Events director Emily Burman presented the strategy she had built with the sponsorship lead, along with the financial position behind it. Much of the discussion covered the contract for the planned Dublin conference, which the venue had not agreed to cancel under force majeure, and the options of moving that event to 2022 at extra cost. The San Francisco Global AppSec contract and its cancellation penalties were also reviewed.

The presenter then went through results from the virtual Global event, where live attendance and on-demand viewing fell well short of expectations and sponsors reported low engagement. Proposed replacements included short lightning conferences with one sponsor each, paid community contests, training courses rerun in other time zones, a regional event in Australia, a hybrid San Francisco option, and executive roundtables. Board members questioned whether sponsors would buy into these formats, the financial risk of running events with weak uptake, and whether sponsored talks could stay vendor neutral.

The board agreed to move ahead with the first training courses and to open a call for trainers. It did not finish the votes on in-person events, because quorum was lost before they were taken. Those decisions were moved to a Doodle poll and to the November board meeting, after staff sound out sponsors. A line of credit was also raised as a way to cover expected shortfalls in 2021.

talks.title: 202104 April 2021 Global Board Meeting
talks.teaser: Follows an OWASP Foundation board meeting on finances, membership, chapter cleanup, bylaw changes and a new outreach committee.
talks.summary:
This is the April 2021 global board meeting of the OWASP Foundation. The session opened with approval of the previous minutes, then moved to a rework of the key performance indicators. The board agreed to drop website traffic figures in favour of mission measures such as active chapters, active meetings and active members, with service-level reporting left to staff. The finance report showed more than one million dollars in cash at the end of March, about twelve months of operating reserve, and lower liabilities than a year earlier. The treasurer also reported that a PPP loan forgiveness application had been submitted and a second application was in preparation.

Operational updates covered a merchandise store run on a dropship model. The board was reminded that gross sales above a set threshold could bring sales tax duties and unrelated business income filings, so the store would be watched closely. A chapter reactivation drive with an April 30 deadline was presented alongside membership campaign results. Discussion also covered a scoring approach for partnership and co-marketing requests, and a proposal to simplify the bylaws' good-standing rules for directors, which led to a volunteer subcommittee being formed.

The board approved the charter for a new Outreach committee and reviewed a draft events committee charter whose officers were still being confirmed. Members agreed to hold shorter, split executive sessions during the year rather than one long session, with a poll to settle dates. The main takeaway is the board's push toward measurable mission outcomes, tighter policy compliance and cleaner membership data.

The executive director reported on finalising the 2021 budget, releasing finance reform policies, setting up trademark work in Australia, and moving staff communications to the community Slack. The treasurer followed with January figures: about $45,000 in revenue, a monthly net loss near $6,000, and cash holding near $50,000.

Board members then voted on several items. A revised chapter policy was approved effective 23 February 2021, and the executive director's signing authority was reset to a $10,000 limit with dual approval. A plan to register trademarks through the WIPO Madrid system, with a budget capped at $15,000, passed, along with motions to formalise eVotes and to allow consent packages for small bylaw changes that need a two-thirds vote. The 2021 budget vote was tabled after questions about marketing funds, and a special meeting was planned to revisit it.

The discussion also covered gendered language in the bylaws, raised through a pull request, along with open issues in the policy repository and how community members can contribute to policy drafts. Participants discussed moving default repository branches to main and turning on branch protection. The meeting closed by moving the next board meeting on 23 March to 12:00 p.m. Eastern.

Shelby walked through the October and November financial reports, which showed year-to-date revenue ahead of budget, largely because income from the Global AppSec San Francisco event was recognised in November. Expenses stayed under budget while final hotel bills were still outstanding, and cash stood at about 2.67 million, roughly 14.9 months of operating reserves.

Lisa reported 6,366 individual members, just short of a 7,000 goal but the highest individual count so far, along with 951 lifetime members and five new chapters. Harold presented a project audit that found no vendor neutrality violations among the flagship projects. The project committee proposed moving three flagship projects to production level, and the board debated whether that call belongs to the board or the committee.

The board passed a motion allowing economy Plus travel for flights over six hours, or a single-step upgrade when it is unavailable. A $10,000 diversity and inclusion scholarship motion was tabled until it is placed in the budget with a clear process. talks.teaser: Reviews OWASP's draft 2023 budget, event finances and membership figures in a November 2022 board meeting.

The November 2022 global board meeting of the OWASP Foundation was held in San Francisco. Shelby presented a draft 2023 budget projecting about $2.7 million in income and a small surplus of roughly $1,000. Conference registrations were budgeted near $850,000 and event sponsorships near $800,000, while individual and corporate memberships were budgeted at $300,000 and $250,000. The board noted reserves of about 16 months, which could support an investment year, and expects the budget to be finalised in December and ratified in January.

The board also discussed the upcoming Dublin event, which was expected to be roughly profitable with ten exhibitors, and a cost overrun of about $45,000 expected from the San Francisco event. Shelby asked for retrospectives after major events so that lessons learned would be kept. The executive director reported that the Form 990 had been submitted early, that fundraising training had been held, and that membership stood at 6,181, up 43 since late October. Chapter growth was smaller, with seven new chapters in the last 60 days, and Meetup reported 112,000 participants.

The board approved the previous meeting minutes by vote, and a project audit was in progress. The meeting closed with the next board session set for December 20, after a November session was cancelled.

The meeting opened with attendance, approval of the prior minutes by a 4-0 vote, and a motion to table the outreach committee's ambassador program until the next meeting. Reports covered a branding refresh with new slide templates and trademark guidance, a new regional chapter policy, and bylaw changes tied to the upcoming election. The board also heard that a candidate's membership had lapsed for 45 days, yet the system showed continuous membership after renewal. The plan was to disqualify him if he ranked near the top and move to the next candidate.

The financial update covered the period through September 30, 2022, showing earned revenue of about $1.2 million and net income near $144,000, well above a budgeted loss of $20,000. Cash reached roughly $2.1 million, equal to about 16.3 months of operating reserves, or 11 months after all expenses. Membership counts were now drawn from Stripe rather than the CRM, which produced a visible dip. Grants were said to take around six months to secure, and Giving Tuesday on November 29 would test peer-to-peer fundraising for flagship projects. Registration for the San Francisco conference stood at 367 attendees, including 65 trainees, and the added marketing spend had reached only $2,369.

Later items covered committee officer elections under the committee policy, a request to revisit that policy, and staff signing authority that could let staff approve smaller corporate supporter agreements. The board also raised sanctions screening for payments and a community manager role, but it deferred funding priorities for 2023 to an in-person meeting. Discussion of a collaboration with the Open Source Security Foundation moved to an executive session. The main takeaway is that budget, grant policy and staffing decisions remain open and depend on the incoming board.

The OWASP Foundation global board met in August 2022 for a monthly meeting focused on governance and finance. The chair opened with approval of the previous minutes and reported a quiet month, including work with CREST on an accreditation program that would share a portion of fees with the foundation. Staff were also checking a record membership count of 6,124 against the membership system, which the chair said was not yet fully trusted as a source of truth.

The main debates concerned process. Board members discussed whether staff or the conference committee should choose keynote speakers, with several arguing that the people organizing an event should make that call. The board then voted to make in-person Global AppSec San Francisco a mask-mandatory event, with members weighing public health rules, staffing burden, attendees who cannot wear masks, and the effect on presenters and sponsors. An amendment to cover all in-person Global events was withdrawn. The board also unanimously agreed to begin ratifying new bylaws through a directors' electronic vote, which needs a super majority of directors.

The treasurer presented a balance sheet showing higher cash and assets than the prior year, corporate membership ahead of budget, and net income above budget. Proposed membership fee increases and free student membership were discussed, but the board tabled them for a separate executive session before the San Francisco event. For practitioners, the meeting shows how a nonprofit's decisions on fees, membership tiers and event rules are made and debated in public.
