talks.title: Threat Model-as-Code - Abhay Bhargav
talks.teaser: Presents a YAML-based approach that ties threat models to automated application security tests in CI/CD pipelines.
talks.summary:
The speaker argues that threat modeling is often produced as a large, static document that is written once a year or less, goes stale in fast CI/CD environments, leans on generic high-level threats, and stays disconnected from engineering work. He contrasts this with infrastructure-as-code tools such as Kubernetes, Ansible and Terraform, where a declarative spec drives the whole deployment.

The proposed approach is ThreatPlaybook, an open-source framework that breaks a model down feature by feature. Each feature starts with a user story, linked to abuser stories describing how it could be misused, then to threat scenarios such as SQL injection or CSRF, and finally to security test cases and mitigations. These are written in YAML and executed through Robot Framework scripts that call tools for Node.js scanning, npm audit and ZAP. Results are correlated back to the threat scenarios by CWE. A recorded demo of an expense-management app showed the pipeline running, with the ZAP scan fast-forwarded. Diagrams and threat maps are generated from the spec rather than drawn by hand.

The takeaway is that a threat model can act as a playbook for application security, guiding test coverage, pentest prioritization and automation, and it can be updated incrementally as features change. The speaker presented this as one option rather than the only way, noted that the project is young, and said a CLI and better diagramming were planned.

talks.title: Fixing Mobile AppSec - Sven Schleier
talks.teaser: Presents the final OWASP MASVS and MSTG, covering Android and iOS testing challenges and the limits of software protections.
talks.summary:
The talk introduces the final versions of the Mobile Application Security Verification Standard (MASVS) and the Mobile Security Testing Guide (MSTG), two OWASP resources meant to give a baseline for complete and consistent mobile app security tests. The speaker explains that iOS and Android offer secure storage and communication APIs, but apps only benefit when developers use them correctly. Areas discussed include data storage, where credentials and sensitive data can end up on the device or in the clipboard, and inter-app communication. Web classes such as cross-site request forgery are noted as rarely relevant to mobile apps, while cross-site scripting can still matter inside app web views.

The middle of the talk covers the work of turning MASVS requirements into test cases for iOS and Android. The speaker describes the challenges of Android fragmentation and the differences between the two platforms, and explains that the guide mixes static and dynamic analysis methods. Network security is illustrated with SSL pinning. Testing a pinned app can involve a jailbroken device or dynamic instrumentation that hooks SSL functions in a running app, which the speaker presents as a more maintainable alternative to jailbreak-based approaches.

The closing part addresses software protections such as jailbreak detection and reverse engineering defenses. The speaker argues these can be defeated over time and should not replace server-side controls, particularly for protecting intellectual property in games. The practical takeaway is to use MASVS to define what must be verified, MSTG to find concrete test methods, and to share security requirements with developers early, since they are often under pressure to ship.

talks.title: A new framework to automate MSTG and MASVS in your CI/CD pipeline
talks.teaser: Shows how to turn MASVS and MSTG checks into BDD tests that run against Android apps in a CI/CD pipeline.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that mobile teams need security checks that run as often as their builds. It proposes combining the OWASP Mobile Application Security Verification Standard (MASVS) and the Mobile Security Testing Guide (MSTG) with behaviour-driven development, so that security tests are written as plain-language Gherkin features with Cucumber steps. Developers and security engineers can then read and review the same tests.

The demonstration used the OWASP MSTG Hacking Playground app, with Calabash driving the UI and ADB handling device-side checks. Two scenarios were shown. The first clears the logs, drives the app, and fails if a username or password appears in the log output. The second checks whether the local database holds a credential in clear text. In the live run both tests failed: the app wrote credentials to the logs and stored an admin password in its database. The results were reported in readable English, and a Jenkins shell step ran the feature files on emulators or devices.

The main takeaway is that tests written this way can catch problems in every build, before a pentest or production release. When a pentester finds an issue that can be automated, it can become a new requirement, a threat-model update and a new BDD test. The speaker noted that the approach is not tied to Calabash and that the project is open source and can be forked. The stated benefits are a security baseline that is always covered and shorter release times when the tests pass.

talks.title: My journey through building an advanced bot detection product - David Senecal
talks.teaser: Traces how a web company built a bot detection product, from scraper defense to behavioral analysis and replay attacks.
talks.summary:
The speaker, a solution architect who has spent about twelve years dealing with automated traffic, describes how a large web infrastructure company built its own bot detection product, starting in 2015 with scraper detection. Early passive checks looked at headers, user agents, reputation and request rate. As bots adapted, the team added active checks such as cookie and JavaScript tests and browser fingerprinting, which caught headless browsers. Fraud such as gift card PIN guessing later led them to add behavioral analysis, acquired through a startup, followed by an SDK for native apps.

Bot operators responded by replaying recorded telemetry, reverse engineering client code, and spreading traffic across large botnets where each node sends only a few requests per minute. The speaker argues that no single method is enough, since each detection technique has blind spots, and that teams must balance false positives against false negatives. Response strategy also matters: serving stale or decoy data can keep bots busy for a while. Attackers have even probed the detection engine itself with floods.

For site owners, the advice is to build a separate login API for each client type, protect every endpoint equally because attackers go after the weakest one, and decommission old APIs. One case involved a retired API that was still live and under attack. Finally, blocking individual bot signatures works only briefly, so tuning detections and acting on them is the better long-term approach.

talks.title: The Anatomy of a Secure Web Application in Java Using Spring Security and Apache Fortress
talks.teaser: Shows how to layer role-based access control, Spring Security and the Java Security Manager in a Java web application.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with the 2017 Equifax breach, which exploited a known Apache Struts flaw, CVE-2017-5638, whose patch had been available for months. Patching alone is not enough, the speakers argue, because unknown flaws always exist. They recommend least privilege and defense in depth, and suggest running a Java application under the Java Security Manager, which is hard to configure but reveals what the application really does.

The middle section covers role-based access control built on the ANSI standard model of users, roles, permissions, sessions, and static and dynamic separation of duty. Apache Fortress implements that model. A sample application applies controls at several layers: container login at the perimeter, Spring Security mapping pages to roles, and programmatic checks in the data access layer, so one layer can catch what another misses. Role constraints tied to a customer context avoid role explosion, where each customer would otherwise need its own copy of a role.

The live demo showed roles being activated to reach pages and data, with errors for out-of-policy access and for activating two roles that violate dynamic separation of duty. Selenium tests cover positive and negative cases. The closing advice is for builders to adopt a standard authorization model like this rather than rebuild it each time, and to test it. Time ran out before the internals were covered.

talks.title: Open Source Security Tools for Kubernetes Applications - Michael Ducy
talks.teaser: AppSecUSA 2018 details Open Source Security Tools for Kubernetes Applications - Michael Ducy.
talks.summary:
### Overview
Michael Ducy from Sysdig presents an architectural and practical overview of open-source security tools for Kubernetes and containerized applications. The talk examines container security through multiple layers, emphasizing the build pipeline and runtime environments. Ducy frames modern container security challenges around the concept of shifting choice to the left, ephemeral container lifecycles, and shared-kernel resource isolation, while demonstrating how open-source tools can enforce policy and automate threat response.

### Key Topics
- **Layers of Container Security**: Security spans underlying infrastructure (host, network, cluster, container runtime), the build phase (source code, dependencies, artifacts), and the runtime phase (secrets, admission, anomaly detection, forensics).
- **Shift Left vs. Choice**: Shifting left should empower development teams with informed choices while establishing automated guardrails such as image analysis and admission controllers.
- **Infrastructure Hardening**: Utilizing core Kubernetes constructs including RBAC, pod security policies, affinity rules, seccomp, SELinux, AppArmor, resource constraints, and network policies.
- **Image Scanning & Build Security**: Employing Anchore Engine within CI/CD pipelines to scan container images, inspect OS/third-party dependencies, and block vulnerable or misconfigured images.
- **Runtime Security & Threat Detection**: Monitoring system calls and orchestrator metadata via Falco to identify abnormal behavior such as spawned shells, binary modifications, and crypto-mining activity.
- **Automated Response Engine**: Leveraging event streams, pub/sub messaging (NATS), and serverless functions (Kubeless) to autonomously remediate threats in real time.

### Technical Details
- **Infrastructure Verification**: Tools like kube-hunter pen-test clusters for exposed endpoints (such as dashboard or kubelet API vulnerabilities), kube-bench audits against CIS benchmarks, and kubesec analyzes deployment YAML manifests against best practices.
- **Network & Service Controls**: Cilium enables Layer 7 network filtering. Spiffe/Spire and service meshes address service identity and admittance, while HashiCorp Vault manages secrets delivery.
- **Anchore Engine**: Analyzes container native artifacts, evaluating OS packages, NPM/gem/Java dependencies, Dockerfile configurations, and hardcoded secrets. It integrates into Jenkins and works with Kubernetes admission controllers (including mutating controllers) to enforce image deployment rules.
- **Falco Architecture**: Falco utilizes a kernel module to capture low-level system call streams, which are filtered using Sysdig libraries and evaluated against rule files containing macros and lists. Out of the box, Falco provides 25 core rules detecting conditions such as writes to `/bin` or `/etc`, shell execution, namespace manipulation, or unexpected outbound connections.
- **Playbooks & SIEM Integration**: In an event-driven setup, Falco alerts publish to NATS topics categorized by severity. Kubeless serverless functions consume these alerts to execute remediation actions, such as killing an offending pod, tainting a worker node, or isolating a pod via network policy. Furthermore, events can be aggregated into an EFK stack (Elasticsearch, Fluentd, Kibana) for dashboarding and forensic review.

### Takeaways
Securing Kubernetes requires automated defense in depth across the build and runtime stages. By validating artifacts early with tools like Anchore and monitoring system calls continuously at runtime using Falco, security teams can establish baseline behavior and trigger automated, granular remediation using lightweight functions without disrupting cluster operations.

talks.title: SCORE Bot: Shift Left, at Scale! - Vidhu Jayabalan - Laksh Raghavan
talks.teaser: Walks through PayPal's deployment of a bot that flags company-specific vulnerabilities in pull requests during code review.
talks.summary:
The speakers describe the problem at PayPal, where more than 4,000 developers work across many languages and internal frameworks. Standard code review tends to focus on style and function, while generic scanners miss company-specific issues such as deprecated internal crypto APIs, problems in logging platforms, and deviations from internal security standards. IDE plugins were hard to keep consistent across many editors, and writing custom static analysis rules took weeks, so the team wanted feedback that arrives within seconds without developers installing or configuring anything.

The solution, called SCORE Bot, runs automatically when a pull request is opened. It scans the changed code and posts a comment that names the affected file, explains the issue in the context of the code, gives step-by-step fix instructions and reference documents, and sends an email with the same details. The merge button is disabled until the finding is fixed or a waiver is requested, and the security team can block releases that contain critical findings. In a live demo, the presenter ran the scanner locally through their developer pipeline tool, then opened a pull request that failed on a deprecated crypto utility and became mergeable again after a waiver was submitted.

The team reported end-to-end visibility across stacks, which lets them spot teams that lag on upgrades and run focused training. Roughly a thousand pull requests were tracked for a legacy C++ stack, with findings trending down over the period shown. The bot returns comments in under a second and runs about 25 checks. The main takeaways are to balance enforcement with developer empathy, to shift checks as early as possible using containerized tools, and to recognise that static checks suit company-specific rules better than dynamic issues. The team also plans to open source a generic rules engine later.

talks.title: Value Driven Threat Modeling - Avi Douglen
talks.teaser: AppSecUSA 2018 investigates Value Driven Threat Modeling - Avi Douglen.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this talk, Avi Douglen addresses the cultural and operational divide between security teams and software developers. With an industry ratio of roughly one security professional for every 100 developers, centralized security teams cannot scale to review every piece of code or architecture change. Traditional threat modeling methodologies—such as STRIDE, Attack Trees, and PASTA—are often too heavyweight, waterfall-oriented, and slow for modern agile sprints. Douglen argues that if security is to scale, developers must perform threat modeling themselves. To make this feasible, threat modeling must shift toward an agile, lightweight approach centered on business value rather than exhaustive attacker modeling.

### Key Topics
- **The Security-Developer Disconnect**: Traditional security approaches demand deep attacker mindset analysis, heavyweight documentation, and weeks-long turnaround times, conflicting with fast two-week agile sprint cadences.
- **Traditional Threat Modeling Frameworks**: Methodologies like STRIDE (Microsoft), Attack Trees, and PASTA (Process for Attack Simulation and Threat Analysis) provide high assurance and thoroughness but do not fit smoothly into lightweight developer workflows.
- **Reframing the Four Core Questions**: Adapting Adam Shostack's four foundational threat modeling questions into value-focused developer questions:
  1. *Why are we building this?* (Identifying business value, revenue, or safety impact rather than just re-analyzing known architecture).
  2. *What needs to happen to make sure we achieve that value?* (Defining explicit conditions and failure states for success).
  3. *How do we ensure those conditions actually happen?* (Translating security countermeasures into explicit functional assumptions, validations, and unit tests).
  4. *Did we do a good enough job?* (Evaluating sufficiency within the agile retrospective).
- **Embracing Useful Imperfection**: Embracing the aphorism adapted from modeling philosophy: "All threat models are wrong, some are useful."Douglen argues teams should lean into this reality by prioritizing immediate usefulness to delivery over unattainable theoretical perfection.

### Technical Details & Implementation Techniques
Douglen outlines concrete integration points for developers within existing agile workflows:
- **Baseline Knowledge & Threat Libraries**: Avoid wasting modeling time on standard code hygiene issues (OWASP Top 10 vulnerabilities like SQLi or XSS, or basic transport layer security) that should be handled by templates, baseline libraries, or training.
- **User Story Integration**: Threat modeling occurs directly during discovery or sprint planning per user story/feature rather than as a standalone document.
- **The "Without" Clause**: Adding a constraint clause directly into the standard user story template: *"As a [role], I want [action], so that [value], without [security catastrophe / loss of value]."*
- **Acceptance Criteria & Definition of Done**: Embedding threat models and explicit security acceptance criteria (e.g., account lockouts after specific failed attempts) directly into user stories and automated unit tests.
- **Abuser Stories & Value Piracy**: Reorienting abuser stories to protect core business assets (e.g., stealing customer orders/juice boxes).
- **Threat Pyramids**: Prioritizing defenses logically—addressing high-impact risks (remote code execution, direct monetary theft) before lower-tier concerns (denial of service, spam).
- **"Sorry Points" for Risk Escalation**: Using a relative risk-scoring mechanism ("sorry points") to measure how disastrous failure would be, helping developers determine whether a story can be modeled independently or requires escalation to security champions or dedicated specialists.
- **Translating Vulnerabilities to Business Impact**: Communicating findings in terms of value (e.g., translating CSRF into "unallocated cash transfers" or authorization bypass into "diverted product shipments").

### Takeaways & Trade-Offs
Value-driven threat modeling offers speed, scalability, native agile integration, and better alignment with developer priorities. However, Douglen acknowledges clear trade-offs: it does not produce complete threat models, lacks high assurance, and may miss subtle threats. High-consequence environments like banking core systems or defense projects will still need rigorous formal reviews. Nevertheless, for day-to-day agile development, empowering developers to perform imperfect, value-focused threat modeling is far superior to performing no threat modeling at all.

talks.title: OWASP Amass Project
talks.teaser: Shows how the Amass project maps an organization's external attack surface through DNS enumeration and network graph visualization.
talks.summary:
The speaker, who leads the OWASP Amass project, explains why it exists. After repeatedly being asked for network diagrams that customers could not provide, he wanted a single way to see an organization's external footprint as an adversary would. Amass focuses on in-depth DNS enumeration to map an organization's namespace. It combines name permutation, reverse DNS sweeping and scraping the internet for names, and it runs passive data sources first before moving to active techniques such as zone transfers, certificate grabbing and brute forcing.

The talk walks through the tool suite, which now includes the core discovery tool, a local transform for an external graph tool, a database handler with Neo4j support, and a visualization tool. A live example shows how each discovered network can feed further discovery, and how the output can be rendered as interactive graphs where structure hints at shared services and relationships between organizations. Recent changes include adaptive rate limiting per resolver and a default mode that needs no API keys.

The closing section covers the roadmap: more consistent results, broader package support, better documentation and video material, and more contributors. Audience questions touched on who uses the tool, with bug bounty hunters, red teamers, OSINT analysts and blue teams all reporting value. The main takeaway is that knowing your external attack surface is a prerequisite for both defending it and assessing it.

talks.title: OWASP IoT Top 10
talks.teaser: Walks through the draft OWASP IoT Top 10 list and the room's feedback on how its ranking should change.
talks.summary:
The speaker introduces the OWASP IoT security project, an umbrella that includes the IoT Top 10, general IoT vulnerability lists, recommendations, an ICS-focused effort and a planned reference architecture. The Top 10 is meant as a list of practices to avoid rather than a strict ranking of vulnerabilities, threats or risks. The draft was built from real-world vulnerabilities gathered from public databases, bug bounty data and contributors' internal findings, weighted by how often each appeared, and checked against many recent IoT guidance documents.

The draft currently leads with weak passwords, followed by insecure network services, insecure access interfaces, insecure outdated components, lack of a secure update mechanism, privacy protection, data transfer and storage weaknesses, physical hardening and device management. Compared with the 2014 edition, passwords moved to the top, cloud, mobile and API access were merged, and storage was folded into transport. The audience pushed back on several points: updatability was argued to be the most important foundation, impact may matter more than ease of attack in industrial settings, access methods could be split again, and supply chain should be named explicitly. Physical hardening and insufficient security configurability were questioned, while root of trust and least privilege were suggested as missing items.

The team treats the list as an open draft and invites further feedback through its OWASP Slack channel. The main takeaway is that the ranking is still changing, with ordering, category merges and manufacturer-focused items all under discussion.

talks.title: Making Security Approachable for Developers and Operators - Armon Dadgar
talks.teaser: Shows how platforms, middleware and frameworks can take security burdens like secrets and encryption off application developers.
talks.summary:
The talk asks why application developers feel security is effortless, and argues that the traditional castle-and-moat model hid network trust from them. That model assumes insiders are trustworthy and the perimeter filters perfectly, and the speaker says both assumptions fail at scale. The Equifax breach, which began with an outdated dependency on a public-facing application, and the Target breach, which spread from an HVAC system across a flat network to databases, show how one foothold can lead to lateral movement.

Zero trust shifts work onto applications. Secrets must be centralized, encrypted and audited rather than scattered across code and wikis, and sensitive data should be encrypted at the application layer, since transparent disk encryption still decrypts for any authenticated query. Services also need caller identity, explicit authorization and encrypted traffic. The speaker shows how cipher documentation overwhelms newcomers with jargon about modes and padding, and notes that code using a zero initialization vector still compiles.

The proposed answer is to split concerns across layers and specialists instead of expecting a super developer. Platforms can deliver secrets and enforce mutual TLS through proxies, key management services can offer encrypt and decrypt APIs so keys never reach application code, and frameworks guard against common web flaws. Security teams can write rules about logical services rather than millions of IP firewall rules. The takeaway is to motivate security by explaining real risks and to accept simpler explanations when people are new.

talks.teaser: Walks through OWASP's chapter and project network, finances, staff roles, and process changes for its leaders.
talks.summary:
This OWASP leaders workshop at AppSecUSA 2018 opened with a level-setting overview of the foundation for chapter and project leaders. It covered the core purpose and values, the three pillars of tools, education and community, the roles of the staff team, and the size of the chapter and project network. Income was shown to come mostly from global conferences and membership, while operating expenses ran above income.

Much of the session focused on money and process. The presenters explained that regional event income is split 90/10 in the foundation's favor, a change from an earlier 60/40 arrangement, and asked the community to help set the right level. They described monthly reconciliation of JIRA tickets and chapter and project balances, accrual accounting that recognizes revenue when invoices are issued, and a planned cleanup of the many event platforms in use. Requests were moving from Salesforce cases into JIRA service desk.

Questions from the floor covered out-of-date wiki entries, a request for a shared email alias for leadership changes, which could not replace named approvers for reimbursements, and a proposal to limit each chapter to three official points of contact. Leaders were told to update the wiki or send changes through the contact form. The takeaway was to keep chapter and project records current and route requests through official channels while the foundation consolidates its systems.

talks.title: Exploiting Unknown Browsers and Objects
talks.teaser: Shows an inspector that enumerates browser JavaScript objects to surface cross-domain and Java bridge flaws.
talks.summary:
Gareth Heyes, a researcher at PortSwigger, starts from a common problem: when a browser or embedded rendering engine ships without developer tools, it is hard to see which objects are exposed and which security protections apply. He presents an Inspector built on his earlier capability-testing page. It ranks interesting objects first, detects window and cross-domain window objects, and identifies function and object constructors, since these can lead to arbitrary code execution or access across origins.

He then goes through bugs that this approach helped uncover. In Safari, overwriting the location host property sent the query string to another origin, and replacing parent and top with alert allowed cross-origin calls. A Microsoft flaw leaked the closed property across constructors, enabling universal XSS. Firefox failed to check the location of a Twitter list page, which exposed user IDs, and a Safari about:blank issue let a local file read content from other sites. For Java bridges in an embedded browser, the Inspector checks for getClass and hashCode, tests whether it can create a socket, and generates a proof of concept. He also showed how a missing annotation check on a referenced object still allowed remote code execution.

Heyes ran live demos of the Java bridge and a Safari exception that leaked an origin. He noted that some checks still need manual analysis, and he described a blind mode for pages that cannot be interacted with, plus uses for probing sandboxes. The takeaway is to enumerate objects systematically and test cross-domain boundaries when no developer tools are available.

talks.title: Prepare(): Introducing Novel Exploitation Techniques in Wordpress
talks.teaser: Shows how design flaws in WordPress core's database helpers enable SQL injection and PHP object injection through plugins.
talks.summary:
WordPress powers a large share of websites, and its core is well covered by a bug bounty program, so the speaker looks at design flaws in the core that plugins can expose. He starts with the built-in defenses, including CSRF tokens, context-aware sanitizers, and WordPress's own prepared-statement implementation. Many plugins depend on that custom implementation because moving them to PDO would require rewriting a lot of code.

The first technique is a "double prepare" pattern, where the output of one prepare call is passed into a second one. In WordPress versions before 4.8.3, a placeholder inside user input could break out of the quoting applied by the second call and inject SQL. WordPress's fix replaces percent signs with a long random token before queries are built. The speaker then shows a second technique that depends on that patch. WP_Query results are cached by serializing the object into the database. A WooCommerce product-list shortcode passes user input into a WP_Query argument, so the token survives serialization and the stored string length no longer matches its contents. By adjusting the length fields, an attacker can inject a PHP object, demonstrated as authenticated remote code execution, and similar patterns were reported in unauthenticated plugins.

The talk closes with a short video of an author-level flaw in media deletion, where thumbnails stayed on disk after the original file was removed, and the speaker explains how this could be abused to reset an installation. For plugin developers, the takeaways are to avoid hand-built SQL with user input, avoid unserialize on user-controlled data, and prefer JSON encoding where possible. Caching whole objects is a core design issue that is hard to remove because of backward compatibility.

talks.title: Serverless Security: Functions-as-a-Service (FaaS) by Niels Tanis
talks.teaser: Explains how Functions-as-a-Service changes the attack surface, monitoring, secrets handling and deployment risks for developers.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from how software architecture has moved from monolithic applications to microservices and then to Functions-as-a-Service, where small, stateless, short-lived functions run in response to events and are billed per execution. The speaker sets out these definitions so the audience shares the same vocabulary, then reviews the benefits, such as no servers to maintain and vendor-managed patching.

The security discussion covers the downsides. A compromised function may only keep persistence for the short lifetime the platform allows, but data can still be exfiltrated. Denial of service shifts from the infrastructure to the application, where heavy event load drives cost and pressure on downstream services. Event-driven chains are harder to map, log and correlate than a single monolith. The speaker points to insecure code in sample applications, including unsanitized log input and SQL injection, and to risky third-party dependencies, such as a compromised npm package. Storing secrets in environment variables exposes them to anyone who compromises a function, so a vault that grants each function only the secrets it needs is preferable. Encryption at rest and in transit, and least-privilege roles instead of wildcard access, are also highlighted.

The closing message is that deployment-as-code pipelines are part of the attack surface and need gates. Threat modeling, isolating environments, monitoring for anomalies and automating configuration help teams act quickly when something changes. The platform abstracts the infrastructure, but it does not remove the need for security design.

talks.title: APPSEC Cali 2018 - Robots with Pentest Recipes
talks.teaser: Shows how to wrap ZAP, Nmap and Selenium tests in Robot Framework keywords to automate application security checks.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at why application security struggles to keep up with continuous delivery pipelines. The speaker describes small AppSec teams being overwhelmed by security reviews, threat modeling and bug bounty triage across many agile teams. Security tools are also hard to automate, since their APIs are often poorly documented or behave differently than described. Custom flaws tied to business logic, such as authorization problems, are usually missed by standard scanners and end up as PDF reports or tickets.

As a proposed answer, the speaker introduces Robot Framework, an open-source keyword-driven test framework, and argues that QA and engineering teams can run security checks alongside their Selenium tests. Tools are wrapped as keywords, with integrations for ZAP and Nmap and others in progress. A demo test suite started ZAP as a proxy, ran login and functional steps through it, launched an active scan, then wrote out a JSON report. A web service example showed the same approach for APIs, where spidering does not work well. Results come out as HTML and JSON with pass or fail status for each step.

The later part covered a pentest pipeline that chains Nmap, a browser login through ZAP and report generation, and the idea of converting a pentester's custom authorization finding into a regression script that fails until the bug is fixed. The speaker also said a large Selenium suite was converted to Robot in a short time and that the scripts can run from Jenkins on a schedule. The takeaway is that teams can turn one-off findings into repeatable checks and lower the barrier for engineers to test for security.

talks.title: APPSEC Cali 2018 - What's New in TLS 1.3
talks.teaser: Explains how TLS 1.3 fixes older weaknesses and cuts handshake round trips, and what 0-RTT resumption costs in security.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from the properties a secure transport protocol needs: confidentiality, authenticity, integrity and forward secrecy. It then looks at why earlier TLS versions failed to deliver them. Previous versions defined a very large number of cipher suites, including weak key exchanges that lacked forward secrecy or server authentication, stream and CBC-mode ciphers with known biases or padding problems, and GCM use where nonce reuse leaked both data and the authentication key. Each case was tied to a known attack.

TLS 1.3 responds by dropping those options. It keeps only five cipher suites, all authenticated encryption modes, and allows only ephemeral Diffie-Hellman key exchange, so forward secrecy is always present for normal sessions. The handshake moves to one round trip by having the client send a key share up front, and the server's certificate and signature are now encrypted. Session resumption uses tickets, but resumed sessions only get forward secrecy if an extra Diffie-Hellman step is added. Zero round-trip early data is shown to lack forward secrecy and to be open to replay, with buffering until the client's finished message offered as one mitigation.

For deployers, the practical points are to keep ephemeral keys on resumption, rotate the ticket encryption keys on a schedule while accepting that old tickets then fail, and take care when sharing ticket keys across a server farm. Early data should only carry idempotent requests, or be disabled where sensitive or state-changing actions are involved. In the Q&A, the speaker noted that middleboxes that mishandle the new handshake have slowed adoption, and that the protocol includes downgrade protection.

talks.title: APPSEC Cali 2018 - MarkDoom: How I Hacked Every Major IDE in 2 Weeks
talks.teaser: Shows how web flaws in embedded browsers of desktop IDEs and editors can escalate to code execution on the host.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at what the speaker calls the desktop web: applications such as code editors and chat clients that render their interface with embedded browser engines, usually Electron. The speaker focuses on markdown previews, since markdown falls back to raw HTML, so a previewed file can inject script into a window with access to the local machine. The question posed is whether an embedded browser is present and whether attacker-controlled content can reach it.

Across editors and IDEs the speaker walked through several cases. Some Electron apps exposed Node integration to the page, and a meta redirect could escape a content security policy set in the page. Remote SMB or NFS shares that auto-mount made a remote HTML file look local, and a crafted AppleScript app bundle or macOS terminal preferences file ran through the system open command without executable-permission checks. JetBrains bridge calls, internal VS Code debugger URLs and file-origin reads in Eclipse gave other routes.

For practitioners, the takeaway is to treat any embedded browser as an attack surface and limit what the page can reach: enable content security policy, turn off Node integration, block navigation, sanitize HTML, and avoid handing links to the OS open command. The speaker also argues that an XSS in a chat application could lead to the same outcome, and that Electron-based apps each ship their own copy of the framework, so updating one does not fix the others.

talks.title: Threat Modeling Toolkit
talks.summary:
The talk presents a practical threat modeling toolkit for application security work. The speaker treats threat modeling as a design-stage activity that clarifies how a system works for reviewers, and stresses that it should be collaborative, since talking through a model with other people is what surfaces mistakes and gaps.

The first component is a simplified flow diagram, drawn with Microsoft-style notation of actors, processes, data stores, flows and trust boundaries. Rather than diagramming everything, the speaker focuses it on the attack surface, labels protocols and adds notes on open questions. A security control checklist sits alongside, marking each control as done or missing so teams can see the gaps against the diagram. The worked example is a personal cryptocurrency setup with a software wallet, a browser, a mobile app and an exchange website and API. While mapping the wallet, the speaker found a JSON-RPC endpoint that answered requests without authentication.

The second component is an attack tree. The attacker's goal sits at the root, sub-goals branch below it with AND and OR gates, and concrete vulnerabilities form the leaves. The example goal is stealing cryptocurrency, which splits into wallet access, exchange access and market manipulation, and the speaker stops digging once a branch is deep enough. Trees can be written as code with PlantUML, which makes them easy to rearrange, and controls from the flow diagram can be mapped onto the sub-goals they mitigate. The main takeaways are to keep the scope narrow, accept that any model will be incomplete, and use these artifacts to bring developers, architects and security staff into the same conversation.

talks.title: Women In Security Panel
talks.summary:
The panel opens with the moderator linking the industry's talent gap to its diversity gap, arguing that sharing career stories can encourage more women and people from minority groups to join. Each panelist then describes how they entered security, from early exposure to computers and volunteering in an IT department to switching careers from hair styling or project management. Their current roles span consulting, start-up security leadership and running their own firm.

The audience Q&A covers finding mentors. Panelists point to formal groups for women in security and privacy, mentorship programs for first-time conference speakers, and reaching out on LinkedIn or Twitter with a specific, personal request rather than a bare greeting. They also suggest seeking mentors from other underrepresented groups, who may understand workplace situations such as credit being taken for one's work. A second question asks how to start a security program at an early-stage company. The answer is to run a gap analysis of products, customers, data and assets, rank the gaps by impact, such as broad cloud access, and reassess progress over time.

When asked about harassment, the panelists described being mistaken for sales staff, an incident at a conference party where bystanders intervened, and the value of speaking up in the moment. They said male colleagues can act as allies by briefly redirecting a conversation when a woman is talked over, and by checking in with colleagues afterward. The session closed with encouragement for newcomers to try security, get connected and stay curious.

talks.title: APPSEC Cali 2018 - Pack your Android: Everything you need to know about Android Boxing
talks.teaser: Explores static techniques to recover malicious payloads from obfuscated, packed, and protected Android applications.
talks.summary:
Malicious Android applications increasingly reach users through major app stores, while authors combine obfuscation, packing, and protector schemes to hide payloads from storefront scanners and analysts. The presentation frames why those layers matter—mangled identifiers, emulator and root checks, anti-debugging, tamper detection, and white-box cryptography—and why dynamic review inside short sandbox windows is easy to evade.

The core walkthrough separates three hardening families and shows how static work can still surface genomes. Lightweight obfuscation may leave ransomware passcodes visible after decompilation; heavier DexProtector-style reflection chains can be walked with helper scripts that reassemble decryption material. Packers that stash or decrypt classes.dex are traced through manifest stubs, oversized headers, multi-dex loaders, patched native libraries, and in one case adb backup of a files-folder dex left on disk between runs. A combined protector case reuses packer logic after peeling SDK-mimicking call paths.

The speaker ties these case-by-case methods to an open effort cataloging dozens of obfuscators, packers, and protectors with per-variant decoders, hundreds of distinct Android genomes, and a planned static analysis engine aimed at broad store scanning. Practitioners should expect manual, sample-specific tooling rather than one maintained universal unpacker.

talks.title: APPSEC Cali 2018 - Hunter - Optimize your Pentesters Time
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in APPSEC Cali 2018 - Hunter - Optimize your Pentesters Time.
talks.summary:
### Overview
At AppSec California 2018, Karen Shirali discussed the challenges eBay faced managing a high volume of penetration testing requests for internal applications and how they optimized tester resources. eBay employs a hybrid model of internal staff and external consultants to handle fluctuating demand across numerous internal developer-built systems and third-party tools. However, roughly 20% to 25% of penetration test report findings were consistently composed of easily detectable, repetitive configuration issues—referred to as "true positive pentest noise"—such as deprecated TLS versions, weak ciphers, and missing or misconfigured security headers. Because documenting and retesting these low-hanging issues consumed valuable consultant time and budget, eBay developed an automated, lightweight pre-requisite tool named Hunter to filter them out before applications enter the pentest queue.

### Key Topics
- **Internal vs. External Pentest Scoping**: External systems like eBay.com have robust context and secure SDLC controls, whereas internal applications vary widely in language and framework, often lack source code access (e.g., COTS software), and are scoped in 2–3 week engagements with external consultants.
- **The True Positive Noise Problem**: Findings like SSL 3.0/TLS 1.0 support, missing cookie flags, or absent HSTS/CSP headers represent real vulnerabilities, but spending expensive consultant hours identifying and retesting them detracts from uncovering critical business logic flaws.
- **Failure of Self-Certification Checklists**: An initial attempt to enforce a manual 10-to-15 item checklist with pre-canned configurations failed because engineering teams lacked security expertise, applied fixes incorrectly, or claimed compliance without effective verification.
- **Pre-Engagement Gating with Hunter**: Developing a fast, simple self-service scanner that grades endpoints and enforces a strict prerequisite (e.g., requiring an 'A' grade before entering the queue) eliminated false claims of readiness.

### Technical Details
- **Tool Architecture**: Hunter is a Python-based application using Django and Django REST Framework. The front end provides a minimal single-input interface where developers supply an HTTP endpoint and receive a letter grade (initially A to C) in under 30 seconds (often 3 to 5 seconds locally).
- **Underlying Scanning Modules**: Hunter incorporates Alban Diquet's `sslyze` (from Data Theorem) alongside additional Python libraries to audit endpoints.
- **Checks Performed**: 
  - Protocol and encryption auditing: Flags SSL 3.0 (with heavy penalty deductions), discourages TLS 1.0/1.1, and verifies TLS 1.2 support alongside cipher evaluations against recommended lists.
  - Security headers: Evaluates Strict-Transport-Security (HSTS), Content Security Policy (specifically catching bypasses like `unsafe-eval`), and cookie security attributes.
- **Scoring Engine**: Implements a weighted deduction model (e.g., SSL versions deduct 20–25% of the total score). Future roadmap items include decoupling scoring rules into an admin configuration, LDAP/SSO integration to persist scan histories, periodic automated re-checks, and internal CA/self-signed certificate verification.

### Takeaways
Enforcing Hunter as a mandatory gate for internal systems dramatically reduced repetitive configuration findings by double-digit percentages. Filtering out this noise shortened pentest durations, minimized tedious retest and remediation loops, lowered external consulting costs, and allowed testers to focus their time and energy on complex business logic vulnerabilities.

talks.title: APPSEC Cali 2018 - How Privacy Violations, Fines and Economic Sanctions Create Darker Opportunities
talks.teaser: Shows how sanctions and GDPR fines can push regimes and criminals toward extortion, using real investigations as examples.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at how economic sanctions and privacy regulation can create new openings for extortion and funding by sanctioned regimes and criminal groups. The speaker draws on investigations they have led. One case involved a state-linked group that targeted a mining exploration firm in East Africa, trying to steal geospatial data and planting cryptocurrency mining software. The speaker argues that digital assets have replaced bulky gold or ivory as a way to move funds, and that extortion is becoming more common.

The middle of the talk turns to the EU General Data Protection Regulation. It covers requirements such as lawful processing, transparency, data minimisation and the need to demonstrate security, along with the risk of large fines that can force a company to disclose its worldwide income. The speaker describes a cyber exercise scenario built around ransomware and extortion against European institutions. A separate case involved an embassy whose weak email password let attackers send extortion demands to other embassies in the same city.

The closing advice focuses on preparation: reduce the personal data collected, anonymise what must be kept, keep printed copies of key information, and know in advance who to call for incident help. The speaker also warns against assuming that paying a ransom ends the matter, since demands often escalate. Common root causes in the cases shown were sensitive data exposure, security misconfiguration and insufficient logging. Free training labs and a shared malware hash platform were recommended as resources.

talks.title: APPSEC Cali 2018 - Taking on the King: Killing Injection Vulnerabilities
talks.teaser: Argues that web apps are string-building compilers, and proposes safer interfaces and context-aware escaping to stop injection flaws.
talks.summary:
Justin Collins frames injection vulnerabilities, including SQL injection, command injection and server-side template injection, as the result of building web applications through string manipulation. He cites OWASP Top 10 rankings and HackerOne and Bugcrowd data to show that injection is relatively uncommon but high-impact when it appears. His core definition is that untrusted data gets interpreted as code by a database, shell, browser or template engine.

The middle of the talk compares a web app to a compiler. A real compiler moves from tokens to syntax trees to intermediate representations, while a web app usually assembles HTML, JavaScript and SQL as text from untrusted inputs. He reviews common defenses: ORMs and parameterized queries help, but placeholders often fail for column or table names, and manual escaping is easy to get wrong. His suggestions include removing unsafe string-based interfaces from libraries, offering typed query and template-composition APIs, restricting input languages where full programming power is unnecessary, and building context-aware escaping into templating engines. He mentions Go templates, PHP auto-escaping and secure Handlebars as examples, and says he found no equivalent for SQL or shell.

He closes by arguing that frameworks should ship injection protections by default, as they already do for CSRF and XSS, and that a secure-by-default library could be wrapped by many frameworks. The talk is presented as a thought piece, and audience questions covered stored procedures, static analysis coverage and third-party data entering databases.

talks.title: APPSEC Cali 2018 - Applied Deception Beyond the Honeypot: Moving Past 101
talks.teaser: Argues that defenders should use deception as a strategic capability, not just honeypots, guided by kill chain and OODA thinking.
talks.summary:
Robert Wood frames deception as a resiliency strategy for defenders rather than a set of honeypots. He argues that many deception products struggle because they are predictable: attackers recognise a tripwire, learn from it, and move on. Using the kill chain and the OODA loop, he explains that each failed attempt teaches an adversary something, so defenders should aim to shape and slow that learning cycle instead of simply blocking.

The talk then compares attitudes toward failure, citing airline incident analysis, a vacuum designer's thousands of prototypes, and healthcare's reluctance to hold blameless reviews, and suggests attackers iterate more readily than defenders do. It contrasts the Russian concealment and disinformation doctrine with the lower-profile Chinese approach, and offers ideas such as applying the honey concept to people, files and databases, and layering controls outward from the assets. The World War II Enigma example shows the Allies reading enemy traffic but acting carefully so the Germans never learned it was broken.

For practitioners, the closing advice is to tie each deception control to a defined strategic objective and a realistic adversary profile, and to start with one small control. In audience questions, Wood suggested framing a tripwire file as a policy violation and warned against flooding the SOC with false positives.

talks.title: APPSEC Cali 2018 - SecDevOps: Current Research and Best Practices
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of APPSEC Cali 2018 - SecDevOps: Current Research and Best Practices.

talks.title: Threat Modeling Panel
talks.summary:
The panel opens with a question on why threat modeling fails and what teams can do to recover. The panelists agree it is a long process rather than a single tool or one-time deliverable. Common failure points they describe include information that does not flow between people, egos turning design reviews into contests, and organizations expecting a purchased tool or a last-minute request to deliver results.

On agile teams, the discussion turns to keeping models current. Panelists suggest treating the model as a living document, revisiting it on defined triggers, and assigning an owner who is notified when completed stories change the attack surface. One example describes a team that updates its architecture diagram each sprint and runs focused threat analysis only on stories that cross trust boundaries. Other points cover version-controlling diagrams, reusable threat libraries for common cloud components, and getting cross-functional teams to explain their own systems at a whiteboard.

Closing advice favors involving the whole development team, including product and project managers, so they take ownership and learn the design through attacker-style play. Tools are only as good as the annotated model put into them, and simple drawing tools can work. Beginners are pointed to free design-flaw guides and to asking an experienced reviewer to critique their work. The main takeaway is to start and iterate.

talks.title: APPSEC Cali 2018 - Lessons From The Threat Modeling Trenches
talks.teaser: Walks through building threat modeling programs at scale, training architects, and rethinking risk scoring beyond CVSS.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at how to build a threat modeling program that lasts, drawing on experience running security architecture teams at several large companies. It argues that design flaws, not only coding bugs, drive many serious failures, and that security staff parachuting into projects just before launch creates friction and rework. The alternative presented is training embedded architects, opening threat model sessions to product, project and development managers, and revisiting the models as the system changes.

The middle section covers governance and quality control. Decentralized programs lose visibility unless documentation is tracked centrally, so the speaker uses a lightweight peer review by two people, escalating only when they cannot agree. Using the Spectre and Meltdown disclosures, the talk asks whether a design could reasonably have anticipated later research, and suggests threat modelers should follow published papers. For prioritization, the speaker warns that CVSS measures vulnerability severity rather than risk, can overstate issues with little attacker value, and recommends FAIR as a more rigorous model. Calling out small risks early is presented as a way to build trust with decision makers.

The closing advice is to study many architectures, learn from enterprise architects, and treat threat modeling as a keystone activity that brings teams into the secure development lifecycle. Practitioners should accept that mistakes will happen while people are trained, avoid routing routine decisions through architecture boards, and keep the program's records accessible as it grows.

talks.title: APPSEC Cali 2018 - Leveraging Cloud SDNs to Solve OWASP Top Ten
talks.teaser: Shows how software-defined networking can chain security appliances into cloud traffic paths without changing IP addressing.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at why security teams struggle to protect workloads in cloud environments. Applications appear and disappear within days or hours, security rules grow more complex, and manually configured appliances lead to delays and errors. Appliances that sit only at the cloud edge also leave traffic inside the virtual network unwatched. The speaker frames the work around a managed security provider's move from physical firewalls and web application firewalls into third-party clouds, and the problems that move exposed.

The middle of the talk proposes virtualizing security functions such as web application firewalls, IDS/IPS, firewalls and load balancers, then segmenting them per application instead of sharing one monolithic set. Pre-built golden images let teams deploy identical security tools with their applications, and automation can attach protection when a virtual machine exposing ports 80 or 443 starts. Software-defined networking service chaining steers traffic through these functions at layer 2, using port pairs, port pair groups and flow classifiers, so application addressing does not change. A hands-on lab built on OpenStack Neutron-compatible networking uses tools such as snort, ModSecurity, squid, tcpdump and pfSense.

The closing takeaways are to use cloud networking primitives for security, bring security into CI/CD by patching and redeploying golden images, and ask vendors for cloud-deployable, consumption-based licensing. Layer 2 insertion is transparent to applications but needs an SDN that supports it. Standardized images per application also help a security operation scale beyond one-off customer setups.

talks.title: APPSEC Cali 2018 - Security After Death -- Not your problem, or is it?
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of APPSEC Cali 2018 - Security After Death -- Not your problem, or is it?.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this presentation at AppSec California 2018, security auditor Tae Shipp addresses the challenge of managing and recovering digital accounts after death or incapacitation. Motivated by personal experience after the death of his best friend Eric Jacobs—whose widow needed assistance recovering account credentials to wind down his digital life—Shipp outlines practical security practices for managing extensive credential inventories, securely sharing sensitive accounts during life, and establishing resilient, multi-party master password recovery procedures.

### Key Topics
- **The Modern Digital Estate Dilemma**: Historically, a death certificate, marriage license, or basic identity information was sufficient to settle bank and legal affairs. In contrast, modern accounts (such as Google, Facebook, and AWS) cannot easily be transferred or closed without account credentials.
- **Password Managers and Vault Selection**: Storing credentials in human memory, physical sticky notes, or cleartext files introduces severe operational and security flaws. While single sign-on / "super federation" creates a single point of failure, dedicated password managers (e.g., KeePass, LastPass, Dashlane, Zoho) allow users to maintain randomized, unique passwords for hundreds of services behind an encrypted master vault.
- **Credential Sharing and Vault Features**: In household and corporate environments, group sharing mechanisms and access tiers (such as "use only" options in LastPass) let users share access without disclosing cleartext passwords. Additionally, vaults can securely store sensitive artifacts including driver's licenses, passports, credit card data, and PKI certificates.
- **Master Password Recovery via Shamir's Secret Sharing**: Relying on a single person or unmanaged master password creates a failure point. Shipp proposes generic secret sharing—specifically Shamir's Secret Sharing—to require multi-person collusion (e.g., 2-of-3 or 3-of-5 schemes) to reconstruct the master password.

### Technical Details
- **Password Complexity and Length**: Shipp recommends generating randomized passwords of at least 20 characters for accounts without multi-factor authentication, avoiding human predictable patterns.
- **Authentication Assurance Levels**: The talk references NIST authentication levels: NIST Level 1 (single-factor password), NIST Level 2 (one-time token generators like RSA and Google Authenticator), and NIST Level 3 (hardware tokens like YubiKey).
- **Shamir's Secret Sharing Scheme**: Based on polynomial interpolation (published by Adi Shamir in 1979), this scheme breaks a master secret into multiple shards where each shard is no longer than the original input secret. Reconstruction requires reaching an established threshold (e.g., $k$ out of $n$), ensuring individual shards reveal no data about the secret on their own.
- **Emergency Recovery Architecture**: An out-of-band recovery workflow involves writing emergency instructions, placing them in an encrypted ZIP file on cloud storage, splitting the archive's passphrase using Shamir's Secret Sharing, and distributing the shards and shared folder access among designated custodians.
- **MFA Backup for Estate Continuity**: When addressing accounts guarded by Google Authenticator, Shipp highlights that photographing or backing up the initialization QR/GIF code into an encrypted vault preserves the seed and clock synchronization data, allowing authorized trustees to restore token generation on another device.

### Takeaways
- Migrate away from browser-default unencrypted password saving, cleartext files, and predictable pattern passwords to a dedicated password manager.
- Implement multi-factor authentication on all high-value services, backing up seed initialization artifacts inside the secure vault.
- Create an out-of-band recovery system using Shamir's Secret Sharing with an appropriate threshold scheme to enforce dual-control collusion among trusted custodians, ensuring your digital estate can be cleanly accessed and resolved upon incapacitation or death.

talks.title: APPSEC Cali 2018 - Decrease Your Stress and Increase Your Reach with Appsec Champions
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of APPSEC Cali 2018 - Decrease Your Stress and Increase Your Reach with Appsec Champions.
talks.summary:
## Overview

Colleen, a security leader with experience since 2005 who built AppSec programs at Twilio (growing the team from 3 to 17 people) and Segment, presents strategies for leveraging AppSec Champions—developer advocates—to scale security programs beyond what a small security team can accomplish alone.

## The Problem

Many well-resourced companies still fail at security, not due to lack of funding but due to over-indexing on "checkbox compliance" rather than meaningful security culture change. Security teams often work in isolation, with developers avoiding consultations, scan results ignored, and AppSec audit failures. The core issue: the traditional security-versus-developers model is broken.

## Why AppSec Champions Matter

People are both the biggest security concern and the biggest asset. By converting developers into security champions, organizations reduce security team burden and ensure developers are included early in solutions. This is critical because fast-moving teams shipping multiple times daily will defeat security controls if not engaged as partners.

## Key Pieces of the Plan

**Prerequisites:**
- Create a visual roadmap showing quarterly/annual goals
- Secure budget for the program (training, rewards, conferences)
- Document the AppSec Champion role and responsibilities
- Identify potential champions (often self-select via security discussions or Slack activity)
- Consult managers about capacity before recruiting champions

**Working with Champions:**
- Establish bi-weekly or regular cadence meetings
- Provide relevant, contextual training on actual vulnerabilities your team faces
- Explain why specific flaws matter; teach prevention rather than just fixing
- Gather feedback on workload and program effectiveness
- Provide active mentoring when champions get stuck
- Reserve space in your own sprint for champion support

**Signs the Program Works:**
- Champions proactively influence their teams to complete security reviews
- Teams schedule threat models and security work without prompting
- Teams consult security before major architecture changes
- JIRA tickets assigned to champions are fixed promptly
- Fewer urgent AppSec incidents occur

## Rewards and Recognition Strategy

Since champions perform extra unpaid work, intentional rewards must align incentives with AppSec goals. Colleen recommends sprinkled rewards throughout the year:

**No-Budget Recognition:**
- Call-out in performance reviews
- Speaking spot at company All Hands
- Public recognition from executives

**Budgeted Rewards:**
- Conference attendance (Black Hat, DEF CON, APPSEC USA)
- Exclusive branded merchandise (t-shirts, stickers via Spreadshirt or Makestickers.com)
- Meetup attendance for security networking
- Physical awards (e.g., Colleen gave a replica Charles V shield costing ~$75-80 to a high-performing team at Twilio)

**Quarterly/Spot Awards:**
- Casual lunches
- Exclusive team swag
- Stickers with designs like "I do what security tells me" or "Security drinks with me because I'm that good"
- Small gift cards
- Unexpected public praise

Colleen emphasizes that meaningful recognition often costs little; people seek acknowledgment, especially when their regular work is mundane.

## Scaling and Remote Considerations

- Each AppSec engineer can manage approximately 6 champions maximum (meaning 6 teams covered)
- For remote developers, use video chat and stagger meeting times to accommodate global schedules
- Implement cascading meetings: champion meets with security, then holds separate meeting with their team to share information

## Champion Selection

Champions need not have formal security training. Look for developers who:
- Voluntarily post security articles or breach news in Slack
- Show genuine curiosity about security
- Are respected tech leads
- May initially resist but can be converted through engagement

Colleen notes that feared "Yolo developers" often become champions, while ostensibly careful developers may push back.

## Positive Outcomes

Beyond roadmap completion, a thriving program results in:
- Developers invested in security and unwilling to let the team down
- Continued progress even during security lead vacation
- Champions actively advocating for the security team
- Cultural shift, even among formerly hostile technical leads
- Long-term relationships and community around security

## Key Takeaways

Security is like a religion; the security leader must create "disciples" to avoid preaching to an empty room. Invest in prerequisites (plan, budget, role clarity, champion identification), provide regular contextual training, mentor actively, reserve sprint capacity for support, reward intentionally and frequently, and trust your champions to advocate and drive cultural change.

talks.title: APPSEC Cali 2018 - We Come Bearing Gifts: Enabling Product Security with Culture and Cloud
talks.teaser: Explains how Netflix's appsec team enables developers with automation, paved roads, and context instead of blocking releases.
talks.summary:
Two Netflix application security engineers argue that a security team can enable fast-moving developers instead of blocking them. They frame the usual adversarial relationship as a problem and describe Netflix's culture of freedom with responsibility and context over control. The model replaces gates with guardrails, so the secure path is also the easy one, and the security team works as a central team inside the infrastructure organization.

Their core idea is a paved road of standardized, templated services, with security controls exposed as simple APIs that teams call. Deployment pipelines in Spinnaker act as the source of truth for an application inventory, so the data stays current without asking teams to fill out surveys. Automated tooling found 36% of ticketed vulnerabilities, and findings are triaged before reaching developers, with only issues tied to plausible attacker positions being raised. Engineers keep the freedom to choose unusual tools, while the team concentrates on high-leverage partnerships and eliminating whole bug classes.

The Q&A covered concerns about unvetted technology, lost visibility, and whether developers will fix findings without pressure. The speakers conceded that developers still sometimes skip security contact and that false positives remain a challenge. Their takeaways were to hook security into developer productivity tooling, to invest in long-term strategic partnerships, and to accept that some risk decisions belong to teams, with a clear escalation path reserved for areas like regulated data.

talks.title: APPSEC Cali 2018 - Breaking Fraud and Bot Detection Solutions
talks.teaser: Shows how browser fingerprinting and behavioural fraud and bot detection scripts can be read, bypassed, replayed and forged.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with the scale of online fraud and automated bot abuse, such as credential stuffing and scraping. It then describes the two common deployment models for fraud and bot detection products: a vendor script loaded by the login page that sends fingerprint and behaviour data to a cloud service for a risk score, and an inline device that injects the same script between the browser and the web server. The threat model assumes the attacker controls the browser and can craft any request or modify any response.

The middle of the talk walks through the weaknesses that follow from running detection logic on the client. The collected signals, which include canvas, audio, font and hardware properties as well as mouse and keystroke timing, can be recovered by reversing the script, even when it is obfuscated. Headless browsers can run the script without a real user. Removing or blocking the script let some requests through, because some deployments fail open. Captured fingerprints could be replayed when they carried no fresh token, and a token computed in client-side JavaScript could be reproduced outside the browser. The speaker also showed that fingerprints can be forged, for example by modifying WebKit to return chosen canvas output, and that a vendor's script domain can reveal its customers.

The closing takeaways are that signals produced in an attacker-controlled environment should not be trusted by the teams that consume them, that protections must cover mobile apps as well as web logins, and that defenders should weigh the limits of these products. The talk ends with questions on privacy overlap, since the same fingerprinting techniques are used for tracking, and on how client-side token generation could be protected.

talks.title: APPSEC Cali 2018 - The Only Reason Security Really Matters for DevOps
talks.teaser: Traces how security programs at eBay and Zynga tied application risk to business value and worked closely with developers.
talks.summary:
The talk opens by asking why organizations do security and why it matters once a company adopts DevOps. The speaker, who has worked on security teams at eBay and Zynga, recounts how each team started. eBay's early team focused on compliance until application security became the priority, since its marketplace let strangers transact online. Zynga's team formed after a run of incidents and ahead of an IPO that required SOX readiness. Both companies ran always-on services at very large scale.

The speaker argues that the security role has shifted from guarding a perimeter to assuming breaches will happen, with more emphasis on logging, monitoring and detection. Security now affects sales, procurement and acquisitions, making it a business driver rather than only a cost. Full frameworks such as BSIMM, ISO standards and the CSA matrix can overwhelm a team, so the speaker reduces the NIST Cybersecurity Framework to three steps: identify, prevent and react. At Zynga, identifying meant ranking bugs on a weekly studio risk profile that weighed bug risk against value to attackers, a view built through threat modeling that studios were taught to run themselves. Prevention included recorded and hands-on developer training, and reaction meant alerting staff to live incidents, which raised trust in the security team.

The takeaways are that security for DevOps must support the business, work collaboratively, and automate only repeatable checks while keeping human-led threat modeling and penetration testing. Trust matters too: the speaker urges security staff to assume engineers are competent and well-intentioned.

talks.title: APPSEC Cali 2018 -Predicting Random Numbers in Ethereum Smart Contracts
talks.teaser: Shows how weak random number generators in Ethereum smart contracts get predicted, and which safer designs avoid it.
talks.summary:
The talk examines random number generators in Ethereum smart contracts, the kind used in lotteries and card games, and explains why their outputs can often be predicted. The speaker manually reviewed 72 distinct implementations collected from a block explorer and GitHub in October 2017, and found 43 of them vulnerable.

Four families of flaws were covered. Values read from block fields such as the coinbase, difficulty, gas limit and timestamp can be reproduced by an attacker's contract making an internal call, so the attacker gets the same result. Block hash misuse came in three forms: querying the current block returns zero, the previous block's hash is known in advance, and blocks older than the 256-block window also return zero. Private storage can still be read from the chain, which broke one lottery whose offset was meant to stay hidden. Transaction ordering enables front-running, where a rival submits a higher gas price transaction after seeing a pending random number.

For safer designs, the talk compared external oracles, which still depend on trusting the oracle service and its data source, and Bitcoin block data as entropy, which makes manipulation harder but does not remove it. Signature-based randomness was discussed, with RSA-based signatures preferred because the ECDSA scheme lets the signer choose a parameter that favours them. Commit-reveal with several participants, ideally combined with a future block hash, was presented as the strongest pattern. The speaker also built a plug-in for a symbolic execution analysis tool to flag transfers controlled by predictable block values.

talks.title: APPSEC Cali 2018 - European Vacation: Leveraging GDPR for Security
talks.teaser: Shows how a security team used GDPR requirements to map data flows, cut retention risk and govern vendors.
talks.summary:
The speaker, a security director at a dating app company, walks through the EU General Data Protection Regulation, which began being enforced in May 2018 and applies to any party processing data on EU residents. He covers the fines, which can reach about 4% of global revenue, and the data subject rights to access, correct, delete, opt out of and port personal data. He argues that the regulation's vague wording on security leaves engineering and security teams with the practical work.

The core practical method is data flow mapping. His team combined a modified parameter-collection tool, run during testing, with static route parsing and the API definitions developers maintain in Swagger, then merged the results into a graph. Each node's colour shows which method found it, which helps judge confidence in a path and exposes outdated API documentation. The same thinking extends to back-end data stores, copies made by downstream services, client-side SDKs that send data directly to partners, and change control so new cookies or pipelines are reviewed before release.

He closes with defensive measures: deleting data that is no longer needed, limiting copies, pseudonymising or encrypting fields where possible, and treating the data export portal as a high-value target, since broken access control there would expose every user. Vendors should sign GDPR addenda, and retention rules must be settled with legal counsel, because laws such as Brazil's retention requirement and anti-abuse needs can conflict with deletion. Backups remain hard, and his suggested answer was compensating controls, such as strong encryption with protected keys.

talks.title: Building a Secure DevOps Pipeline
talks.teaser: Explains how an AppSec team can build an automated pipeline that triages, tests and tracks findings alongside DevOps.
talks.summary:
Matt Tesauro and Aaron Weaver argue that application security teams should borrow the working methods of DevOps, Agile and continuous delivery rather than resist them. The talk opens with an analogy to how railroads shrank travel times across the United States, then compares that shift to the smaller, more frequent software changes teams now ship. The core proposal is an AppSec pipeline whose output is security results rather than built software. Requests come in, get triaged by risk, pass through testing, and land in a normalized vulnerability database that feeds reporting and bug trackers.

The speakers describe how their first iteration focused on making a small team efficient. Tasks that need no human judgment, such as configuring a DAST scanner, were automated, which improved consistency, status tracking and metrics. Later steps connected the pipeline to outside development teams through REST calls, webhooks and Jenkins builds. They stressed that false positives must be avoided in build-breaking checks, suggested running simple health checks such as header and cookie tests on a schedule, and proposed turning a confirmed finding into a regression test that turns green once fixed. Chat-based tooling was presented as a way to reach developers.

Two case studies were shared. One company turned findings into regression tests and assessed 35 applications in a year with two FTEs. The other grew its assessment count from 44 to over 200, then to 414 the following year, even as it lost staff. The speakers closed by urging AppSec staff to write some code, even simple glue code, so they understand the work developers face.
