talks.title: Practical Dynamic Application Security Testing within an Enterprise
talks.teaser: Shows how to put dynamic application security testing into CI pipelines and run passive scans on production URLs from logs.
talks.summary:
Dynamic application security testing, or DAST, is presented as a way to build application security into a CI/CD pipeline without slowing builds. The speaker contrasts black-box scanning of a deployed application with pipeline runs where functional test cases drive a scanner through a proxy, so tests can start during development. The team explains that manual pen tests cannot keep pace when releases ship several times a week, and that scan results need to reach developers quickly.

The second method, called operational security testing, pulls URLs from logging tools and runs quick passive scans against production. Because no attacks are injected, it is considered safe on live systems. It flags misconfigurations such as cookies missing the secure flag or TLS not being enabled, but it will not catch injection or cross-site scripting. A security dashboard calls a bulk scan API, and a controller groups URLs by application and starts scanner containers tagged with scan and application IDs. Status and results endpoints feed findings back to the dashboard and to Jira, and individual scans can be paused or stopped.

The stated requirements were speed, safety, non-invasiveness and autonomy. The approach is scanner-agnostic, so ZAP or any other passive scanner can be used, and the speaker notes that APIs are not yet supported. The takeaway is that passive scanning complements full active scans, can run several times a day across development, staging and production, and gives developers per-application reports without taking time from their pipelines.

talks.title: Capture the Flag for Developers
talks.teaser: Explains how to design a capture-the-flag event that lets developers exploit web flaws hands-on.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that capture-the-flag exercises can teach developers application security better than computer-based or instructor-led courses, because people remember what they actually exploit themselves. The speaker, who has run these events for his own company, walks through the decisions an organizer has to make before running one, from choosing the target application to setting up the infrastructure.

Building a custom vulnerable application is discouraged. It is hard to balance difficulty, and it tends to break at the worst moment, as the speaker learned when his own environment failed the night before an event. Taking a working open-source application and reintroducing bugs is an option, and the OWASP vulnerable web applications directory lists ready-made deliberately vulnerable apps. For developers, the speaker recommends giving breadcrumbs, helper pages or listener commands for exploits, flags stored in a separate cookie or a planted message, and a progression from unprivileged access toward a final operating-system-level challenge. Scoreboards can double as hints. For infrastructure, he suggests a separate wired network or cloud virtual machines rather than corporate Wi-Fi, and a shared base image such as Kali so that setup problems do not eat class time.

Drawbacks include cost, a full day away from coding, and coverage of only three or four vulnerability types. The payoff is that developers who exploit a flaw themselves start viewing their own code from an attacker's perspective, which changes the security culture. The talk closes with an idea for a continuous monthly challenge series with small rewards.

talks.title: Moving Fast and Securing Things
talks.teaser: Shows how a small product security team scales secure development with self-service checklists and developer trust.
talks.summary:
The talk describes how a product security team keeps pace with a fast-growing collaboration company that deploys code many times a day. The team has only three people, so it cannot review every change, and a traditional stage-by-stage secure development lifecycle did not fit the pace. The team chose transparency and trust instead, treating security as an opt-in step supported by regular office hours and public channels.

The core of the approach is a self-service secure development lifecycle. Developers answer an adaptive risk questionnaire about their feature, which generates a tailored checklist of short statements to complete before release, inspired by aviation checklists. Completed checklists alert the security team with a risk rating used to prioritise reviews, and checklist answers reveal where teams misunderstand a concept. Feedback from developers and bug bounty reports keeps the checklists current, and the questionnaire is built as a plugin architecture so new languages can be added easily.

Over the year, the team reported that SDL submissions grew while valid bugs fell slightly, despite more code shipping. Next steps include open-sourcing the framework and checklist content, which they say mostly generalises, and building tooling to detect issues in code automatically. Practitioners can take away keeping checklists concise and specific, making the process searchable and transparent, and revising checklists based on real findings.

talks.title: Secure Product Lifecycle (SPLC) as a Service
talks.teaser: Shows how a small security team turned static analysis into a service that engineers never have to log into.
talks.summary:
The talk covers how a security team inside a large software company's digital marketing unit built a secure product lifecycle, or SPLC, that engineers could follow without much extra effort. The speakers explain that the early problem was a scanning tool offered to teams that few used, because each team had to run its own scans. A small team also could not manually handle the reporting that compliance and product leaders wanted. They describe mapping the SPLC to concrete activities and assigning a security champion on each product team, backed by training and a recognition program.

The main case study is static analysis as a service. Source code is pulled from the repository on a schedule that can be per commit, weekly or monthly, then scanned and parsed by an automation platform designed to accept any input, such as dynamic scanner results or manual pen test findings. Results go out as an email summary to interested parties and as issues in the team's Jira. Repeated findings of the same problem within one file are grouped into a single issue, so engineers fix it once instead of closing dozens of entries. Because teams did not have to change how they work, adoption was reported as complete once scanning became a requirement.

For practitioners, the takeaways are to pilot with one team, refine the process, and then phase in other teams so the system can handle the load. Meeting developers inside the tools they already use matters more than adding another portal. The speakers say these changes built a partnership culture, which freed time for activities such as a champions summit and a hacker village where people practice pentesting.

talks.title: Leveraging the ASVS in the Secure SDLC
talks.teaser: Shows how one healthcare company turned OWASP ASVS verification statements into developer security controls.
talks.summary:
This talk describes how a healthcare company used the OWASP Application Security Verification Standard (ASVS) to push security requirements into its software development lifecycle. The speaker argues that health records are valuable on the black market and that defects caught early are far cheaper to fix than those found in production. The ASVS groups its verification statements into 16 domains across three levels, with level 1 for any application, level 2 for applications handling sensitive data, and level 3 for the most critical systems.

Many statements are hard to test as written, so the team rewrote each one as a control developers could act on, splitting some into two. Controls were grouped as functional (testable with a test plan), process (needing an input and an output artifact), DevOps (requiring operational support) or tech design (documented by architects with links to code). A questionnaire, adapted from an open-source vendor assessment tool, sets the application's level and filters out inapplicable controls, such as authentication when it is offloaded. The remaining controls become tasks in the existing Jira queue, and the full rewritten set totals about 240.

The speaker highlights a shared framework that makes teams comparable, helps prioritize critical items, and raises developer awareness. Wording controls so that testers, designers and security staff read them the same way remains hard, so the team mixed roles and wrote supporting guidance. He presents the work as an ongoing, multi-year rollout rather than a single phase of the SDLC.

talks.title: OWASP BeNeLux Day Attribute Based Access Control. Why, what, how? by Jacoba Sieders
talks.teaser: Explains how a bank moved from role-based to real-time attribute-based access decisions using context and trust levels.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at attribute based access control, the idea of deciding access in real time from attributes rather than fixed roles. The speaker, who leads identity and access management at a large Dutch bank, explains the pressures behind it: open APIs required under payment services rules, data flowing between organisations, and customers whose digital identities pass through many lifecycle statuses and delegated relations.

The middle of the talk covers how the bank built its approach. A trust level framework links the risk of the login context to the risk of the transaction across ten levels, so weaker context reduces what a user may do rather than simply blocking them. Policy decision and enforcement points draw on rule sets and attributes from a user profile database and federated identities. The speaker also described a proof of concept for automated data classification, which matched human classification in about 95 percent of 2,500 scanned documents, with most errors tied to poor scan quality. Clashing rules and rule ownership were presented as a governance problem.

The closing takeaways are that attribute based control works best as a hybrid alongside roles, since migrating legacy systems completely is nearly impossible. Rules should be tested by working backwards from the outcome you want, and business involvement and user education were described as the hardest and most important parts. The project was a five-year effort, and the speaker said it was in year three.

talks.title: OWASP BeNeLux Day A Series of Unfortunate Events: Where Malware Meets Murphy by M. van Ommeren
talks.teaser: Follows a ransomware recovery on Windows file shares, from path-length limits and locked permissions to restoring files from backup.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at a ransomware incident from the victim's side rather than as a standard response playbook. The speaker describes a sample that appended an email address to encrypted filenames, left no usable ransom note, and whose support mailbox never delivered replies. Listing the encrypted files gave inconsistent counts, because Explorer and PowerShell hit the 260-character path limit of legacy Windows file APIs, while mapped network drives shortened the paths on the file server.

To work around this, the speaker mapped the share to a drive letter, used icacls to take ownership where explicit denies blocked access, and used robocopy, which supports long paths and can run with backup rights, combined with PowerShell to copy files past the limit. The backup was a full copy of about one terabyte across more than 100,000 files, and the backup tool could not restore selected files. Restoring over a 40 megabit connection would take more than 35 hours, so a hard drive was shipped and restored locally in about four hours. Saved permissions were reapplied after the restore.

Some encrypted files had only been partly overwritten, so they could not be found by modification time. The speaker located them with an entropy check on the first kilobyte of each file, comparing it with the rest of the file. The takeaways are to test selective restore in backup tooling, plan for path-length problems, place canary files with filesystem auditing to catch encryption early, and not assume helpdesks or tools behave as designed.

talks.title: OWASP BeNeLux Day Exploring the ecosystem of malicious domain registrations in the .eu TLD
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of OWASP BeNeLux Day Exploring the ecosystem of malicious domain registrations in the .eu TLD.
talks.summary:
### Overview
This presentation details joint research conducted between a research lab at KU Leuven and EURid, the registry managing the .eu top-level domain (TLD). The study investigates the ecosystem of malicious domain registrations within .eu, specifically focusing on how malicious actors register domains in bulk to support hit-and-run campaigns (e.g., spam, phishing, command-and-control). Analyzing 824,000 first-time registrations collected over a 14-month period, the researchers set out to identify recurring patterns across registrant data, evaluate campaign behaviors, automate campaign discovery using machine learning, and build proactive detection and prevention mechanisms at registration time.

### Key Topics
- **Bulk Registration and Hit-and-Run Dynamics:** Malicious actors rapidly rotate through domain names to evade blacklisting; prior literature cited showed 60% of malicious domains are discarded after just one day. In this study, 75% of malicious domains were blacklisted within 5 days, and 98% within 30 days.
- **Dataset and Ground Truth Enrichment:** The dataset comprised 824,000 initial registrations from EURid (transfers and re-registrations were excluded). External ground truth was established by querying three blacklist feeds—Spamhaus, SURBL, and Google Safe Browsing—identifying approximately 2.5% (~21,000 domains) as malicious. Name server locations were enriched using the MaxMind Free database.
- **Campaign Identification:** A campaign was defined as a set of malicious registrations sharing common patterns attributable to the same actor over time. Using registrant contact information (names, email addresses, phone numbers, street addresses), registrar usage, and registration spikes, 20 distinct campaigns covering up to 2,000 domains each were manually identified.
- **Behavioral Patterns and Facilitators:** Attackers showed distinct temporal behaviors, including concentration during normal business hours/weekdays and noticeable seasonal dips (summer, Christmas, spring breaks). Registration facilitators exhibited high concentration: a single registrar accounted for 50% of all malicious registrations (with over one-third toxicity), and the top three registrant email addresses accounted for roughly 70% of malicious registrations.
- **Machine Learning and Proactive Prevention:** The team applied agglomerative clustering to evaluate automated campaign discovery against manual findings, and developed a predictive classifier combining clustering and reputation scoring to block malicious registrations at submission time.

### Technical Details
- **Campaign Characteristics:** Identified campaigns varied from short, intense bursts (e.g., 2,000 registrations in 37 days) to long, low-rate campaigns (154 registrations across 300 days). Campaign C11 operated over 8 months with ~1,200 flagged domains, recycling a private email domain with two email accounts, three phone numbers, two street addresses, and four registrars sequentially.
- **Blacklist Expansion:** Examining campaign domains that were not flagged by external blacklists (~4,000 domains), manual verification revealed that less than 1% were false positives, showing that campaign-level clustering can expand existing blacklists by roughly 20%.
- **Evasion and Obfuscation (Campaign C15):** The most sophisticated campaign utilized an identity generation tool seeded with Dutch data (and English surnames) to generate 98 fake registrant identities registering ~500 domains across 258 days. Domain names combined Dutch vocabulary words with occasional typo binding letters, registered in distinct batches of 8, 16, 24, or 32. This campaign fragmented into numerous small clusters, evading standard top-cluster identification.
- **Clustering Evaluation:** Agglomerative clustering produced 432 clusters, with the 30 largest covering 92% of the dataset. Comparing these to the 20 manual campaigns revealed that 26 clusters mapped 1-to-1 to campaigns, while several campaigns shared single clusters, indicating that the 20 manual campaigns actually stemmed from approximately 17 distinct actors.
- **Real-Time Detection Results:** Combining agglomerative clustering with reputation scoring of phone numbers, emails, and registrars allowed early detection of 60%–70% of malicious domains at registration time with an extremely low false-positive rate (approximately two to three registrations per day).

### Takeaways
Attackers rely heavily on specific registrars, free or private email providers, and synthetic registrant identities composed of reused components. Because external blacklisting has a latency window of several days, post-facto blacklisting alone is insufficient. The research demonstrates that combining manual domain intelligence with agglomerative clustering and reputation classifiers enables registries to block or challenge between 60% and 70% of malicious registrations at registration time, a capability EURid is deploying via its Trust and Security program to raise the cost for malicious actors.

talks.title: OWASP BeNeLux Day Don't trust the DOM: Bypassing XSS mitigations via script gadgets by S. Lekies
talks.teaser: Shows how legitimate library code turns harmless-looking HTML attributes into script execution, defeating XSS filters, sanitizers and CSP.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from the idea that common XSS defenses (web application firewalls, browser XSS filters, HTML sanitizers and Content Security Policy) work by blocking malicious markup rather than preventing the underlying flaw. It introduces "script gadgets": legitimate JavaScript already on a page that takes benign-looking markup, such as a data attribute, and turns it into executable code. Examples include a Knockout data-bind attribute that acts like eval, and a Bootstrap tooltip option that switches its content to HTML. Because the attacker's payload is only plain data, the filters and firewalls have nothing to flag.

The research then covers 16 popular JavaScript libraries and checks which gadgets get past each mitigation. Bypasses were found in most of them, including DOMPurify and Closure sanitizers, and expression languages in frameworks such as Aurelia could reach the window object and even insert a nonce. A large-scale scan of the Alexa top 5,000 sites found gadget-related data flows on about 82% of them, and a manual review of around 100 of those flows showed that most were exploitable.

The root cause is the string-based DOM APIs such as innerHTML and eval. The proposed fix is Trusted Types, which replace string inputs with typed values that only safe builders or sanitizers can produce, with a polyfill for older browsers. The main open problem is how to support legitimate "unsafe" conversions, and the team invites JavaScript developers to help shape the feature.

talks.title: OWASP BeNeLux Day The evil friend in your browser by Achim D. Brucker
talks.teaser: Examines how browser extensions undermine web security guarantees through permissions, store-scale analysis, and real abuse cases.
talks.summary:
Modern browsers now carry the same kinds of security-critical workloads operating systems once did, from webmail and banking to enterprise ERP interfaces. Vendors invest heavily in same-origin policy, content security policy, cookie flags, and tab isolation, yet users routinely add extensions that run inside the browser with privileges comparable to an insider attacker.

The presentation walks through what extensions can do in principle—read and alter requests before transport encryption, tweak headers, and effectively neutralize CSP or cross-origin protections—then grounds that risk in store-scale measurement. A recurring crawl captures Chrome Web Store metadata and source for on the order of 80,000 extensions, with dynamic instrumentation and automated browsing used to see what they actually touch. Roughly three fifths of analyzed extensions seek broad site access; about one in ten can intercept and rewrite all web traffic. Case studies span privacy resale (including URL parameters deanonymizing users), monetization tricks, forced-install flows, cryptocurrency mining waves after public disclosure, silent affiliate link rewriting, and analytics injected into every visited page.

For practitioners, the talk argues that extensions belong in threat models as deliberate software installation, not as harmless accessories. Mitigations discussed include scrutinizing authors and permissions, limiting host access to what the feature needs, separating high-risk browsing into dedicated profiles, and organizational approaches between permissive auto-update and strict allow lists, alongside longer-term browser hardening around permissions and sandboxing.

talks.title: OWASP BeNeLux Day Common REST API security pitfalls by Philippe De Ryck
talks.teaser: Covers common REST API security mistakes, from HTTPS and JWT handling to access control, CSRF and CORS.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at common security pitfalls when web applications expose REST APIs, treating them as familiar vulnerabilities appearing in a new setting. It starts with transport security: serve the API only over HTTPS, avoid redirects from plain HTTP where the domain only hosts the API, and send an HSTS header so browsers refuse downgrades. It then covers access control, where an endpoint that checks login but not object ownership exposes other users' data. The example given is a mobile provider that returned account details for any phone number.

The middle section moves to session state and tokens. Client-side sessions must be integrity-checked and, if they hold sensitive data, encrypted, because the server no longer trusts only its own copy. A frequent JWT mistake is calling a decode function instead of a verify function, which accepts tampered tokens. The speaker explains shared-secret versus public/private key signing and warns against sharing signing keys with other applications or clients. Cookies and the Authorization header are compared: the header is not attached to image or script requests, and an Angular interceptor can send tokens to third-party domains unless allowed domains are listed. For cross-site request forgery, the talk covers anti-CSRF tokens, custom headers and content-type checks for APIs that still accept cookies.

The closing part argues that input validation is a useful first line of defense but not a substitute for parameterized queries, since valid-looking input such as names can still be dangerous. The speaker ends by urging attendees to question assumptions when moving to new architectures and to share security experience with colleagues.

talks.title: Monitoring Application Attack Surface and Integrating Security into DevOps
talks.teaser: Shows how mapping a web app's attack surface from source code can focus dynamic security testing inside DevOps pipelines.
talks.summary:
The talk explores how knowing a web application's attack surface can help security teams focus limited testing and fit it into a DevOps pipeline. The speaker defines the attack surface as the places an outside party can reach with input, mainly URLs, parameters, HTTP verbs, headers and cookies. Pipeline security checks get a short window, often 8 to 12 minutes per build, so scanners need a precise target list.

The work grew from research that merged static and dynamic results. The engine reads the source code and framework, such as a Ruby on Rails app, to build an endpoint database. That list helps scanners reach pages a crawler misses, like multi-step forms, hidden parameters and REST APIs. Comparing two git commits shows new, removed and modified surface, and the speaker suggests a percentage change could trigger testing.

In a demo, a watcher on a git repository rebuilt the surface on each commit, posted changes to chat, and ran a scan limited to a newly added page, which surfaced a cross-site scripting issue filed in Jira. The speaker stresses this complements, rather than replaces, manual testing, threat modelling and penetration tests. The takeaway: test new surface first and push results into the tools developers already use.

talks.title: Test Driven Security in the DevOps pipeline
talks.teaser: Shows how Mozilla wires automated security baseline checks into CI and deployment pipelines so issues are caught before production.
talks.summary:
Jo, who manages a Firefox operations security team at Mozilla, argues that manual reviews cannot keep pace with teams shipping code several times a day. The talk opens with bug bounty reports of long-known flaws such as reflected cross-site scripting, which still reach production despite well-understood mitigations like output escaping and Content Security Policy. The goal is to catch such issues before deployment rather than after outside researchers report them.

The middle covers a typical DevOps pipeline of commits, continuous integration, container builds and staged deployments, and a four-step method for testing security within it. Teams first define a security baseline that every release must meet, such as HTTP security headers, cookie flags, TLS settings, log retention, admin panels kept off the public internet, and dependency updates. Each item must be testable so it can run continuously. Examples include a one-minute headless OWASP ZAP scan run against staging, a Bandit scan of Python source, and a check of infrastructure firewall rules that blocks promotion when a database is exposed to the internet. ZAP can also run inside CI against pull request builds, giving developers findings before code is merged.

The closing point is that automated checks free security engineers for harder problems and cut the time spent triaging, fixing and redeploying repeat bounty findings. Manual testing still has a role, but routine checks should be automated.

talks.title: Embedding GDPR into the SDLC - Steven Wierckx
talks.teaser: Shows how GDPR privacy obligations can be mapped onto a secure software development lifecycle using OWASP SAMM.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from the point that GDPR is an EU regulation, and that its definition of personal data reaches further than many organisations expect, including identification numbers and work email addresses. It then walks through the regulation's seven principles and explains which of them legal teams usually own and which affect developers, especially privacy by design and by default.

The middle section maps GDPR articles onto the twelve practices of the OWASP Software Assurance Maturity Model, covering governance, design, implementation, verification and operations, with three maturity levels for each. Privacy impact assessments are presented as a variant of threat modeling that asks what can go wrong with personal data. Testing validates the controls, and monitoring is treated as the point where a breach should be detected and escalated. The speaker describes a project that turned these actions into user stories across sprints, with security champions inside development teams and close work with the data protection officer.

The closing part covers the risk of non-compliance, including possible fines, and lists success factors: build relationships with legal, the data protection officer and the security team early, and fold GDPR tasks into the existing lifecycle rather than running them separately. The material has been contributed to an open-source OWASP project, and workshops were offered to people who want to adopt it.

talks.title: Handling of Security Requirements in Software Development Lifecycle
talks.teaser: Presents an open-source tool that maps OWASP ASVS requirements to artifacts and tracks their implementation through Jira.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from the problems of running security inside agile teams: security groups are understaffed, developers have little spare time for extra steps, and architecture reviews often rely on gut feeling because documentation is thin. The speakers also argue that security requirements are often defined in a waterfall style that falls behind sprint retrospectives, that standards keep changing, and that outsourced development is handled differently from internal work.

Their answer is a requirement automation tool that works per artifact rather than per project. A team describes an artifact by parameters such as criticality, type, authentication and reachability, and the tool returns the matching ASVS requirements. In one example, 107 of the 182 requirements applied, so 75 were removed from the development team's list. Teams record their strategy for each requirement, export the results to Jira, and create tickets in batches, with versioned YAML attachments and notices when the standard changes. A companion compliance automation tool runs checks against a URL, a Git repository or SonarQube, combining scanners such as OWASP ZAP with source code review and reporting a confidence level for each result. The same requirement set can also generate training slides and feed dashboards that show the age of requirement definitions.

For version two, the team plans to integrate the testing directly into the main tool, add rule sets that mark requirements a technology stack already handles, provide language-specific guidance, and support more ticket and chat systems. The practical takeaway is to define requirements for each long-lived artifact and to run gap analysis on important production systems before problems accumulate.

talks.title: Securing C code that seems to work just fine
talks.teaser: Shows how a fast-growing edge company secured its C code using sanitizers, continuous fuzzing and shared operational security.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at why C code that appears to work can hide serious security flaws, using a fast-growing edge computing company as its running example. The speaker links the optimism common in startups to faster growth and to gaps in security. As a case, he recounts the 2015 Stagefright bug in an Android media parser, where an integer overflow in a chunk size calculation let a crafted file trigger a heap overflow. The first patch still failed, because its bounds check was affected by the same wraparound.

The middle of the talk covers practical controls. Clang provides a shared framework for security tools such as UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer, which catches undefined behavior at runtime. The company builds production code with GCC, but its CI also builds with clang and several sanitizers, and a pull request cannot merge unless both builds pass. For testing, the speaker contrasts heroic fuzzing, which fades once bugs are found, with continuous fuzzing that developers own. The team adapted OSS-Fuzz for private repositories, kept fuzzing progress between runs, and ran the cluster largely by hand, reporting high and critical bugs before release.

The closing section argues that security must also cover code running in production, since failures reach the field. Customer-facing and operations engineers can be trained to recognize and report likely memory corruption, and security staff should take part in incident response. Thanking people who report false positives keeps reporting going. Treating each control as an investment with ongoing support costs helps teams choose what to build, and starting with a minimal version lets them iterate.

talks.title: Popular Approaches to Preventing Code Injection Attacks are Dangerously Wrong
talks.teaser: Argues that runtime and compiler techniques, not heuristics or training, can remove code injection bug classes from applications.
talks.summary:
John Matthew Holt, a just-in-time compiler engineer who has worked on the Java HotSpot JVM, argues that application security has been relying on the wrong tools for code injection. He criticises developer training, pattern matching, allow-lists and deny-lists as approximations that cannot guarantee results, and he notes that patching is slow in practice, since organisations struggle to update every Java version in use. He compares the situation to memory bugs of the early 1990s, which largely disappeared once garbage collection became reliably accurate.

The middle of the talk presents runtime techniques. Taint tracking combined with lexical and syntactic analysis can flag SQL injection, cross-site scripting, path traversal and command injection deterministically, the speaker says, with a one to two percent performance cost and no false positives across hundreds of production applications over two years. Randomising Java class namespaces, inspired by address space layout randomisation, makes it hard for injected code to reach classes such as process builders. Confining deserialization APIs to their expected contract, such as allocating objects and linking them into a graph, is another way to block behaviour outside that contract.

For a practical case, the speaker describes a denial-of-service bug in Apache code caused by a missing bounds check. Instead of waiting for a new artifact to be rolled out, a rule written for the compiler was applied as a virtual patch and reloaded without stopping applications. It was delivered within 24 hours and all affected applications were covered within 48. He closes by urging security teams to bring runtime and compiler engineers into the conversation.

talks.title: How to detect CSRF vulnerability, reliably?
talks.teaser: Explains why scanners miss CSRF flaws and presents a small test that checks anti-CSRF token defenses in a pipeline.
talks.summary:
The speaker, who works at a financial services firm, explains why his team needed automated dynamic application security testing as they moved toward CI/CD. With little prior experience, he built a small test banking web application and used it to compare open-source scanners, Arachne and ZAP, along with a commercial product.

The demo form was vulnerable to reflected cross-site scripting and to CSRF. The scanners picked up the cross-site scripting, and that finding disappeared once output encoding was enabled. None of the tools detected the CSRF flaw reliably: Arachne missed it, while ZAP kept reporting it after a fix was applied. The commercial product gave similar results. The speaker argues that a scanner cannot reliably identify an anti-CSRF token among many hidden fields, nor confirm server-side validation by comparing responses, because a failed validation can look like an ordinary business-logic error.

To address this, he presented a roughly 50-line headless-browser test that needs two details agreed between application and scanner: the exact token field name and the exact error response returned when token validation fails. The test checks in order whether the token exists, whether it has a value, and whether the server validates it, reporting which step failed. He recommends sending the validation error before other checks, standardizing token names and error responses across forms, and building such tests into a suite that runs in a pipeline. He notes that production errors should stay generic. The code is shared on GitHub.

talks.title: Making Vulnerability Management Less Painful with OWASP DefectDojo
talks.teaser: Shows how DefectDojo consolidates scanner findings, automates reports and metrics, and syncs issues to ticketing systems.
talks.summary:
Greg Anderson, a senior security engineer at Pearson and the creator of DefectDojo, opens by describing how much application security time goes into reports, metrics and merging output from several scanners, often by hand in spreadsheets. He shares Pearson's own numbers: 44 assessments in 2014 with about a dozen testers, 224 in 2015, and 414 in 2016 after the team moved to DefectDojo, while the team shrank. He describes the overall rise as roughly 840 percent.

He then explains the data model, which runs from product types to products, engagements, tests, findings and endpoints, and follows it with a live demo. The demo covers importing a ZAP XML scan, re-uploading a scan to automatically close fixed findings, generating standard reports from a drag-and-drop builder, and reviewing a metrics page. He also covers deduplication and false-positive history settings, warning that the latter can hide a real issue that matches an old one on the same endpoint. Bidirectional JIRA sync is shown, and he argues that pushing issues into developers' backlogs got far more attention than sending a report over the fence.

He closes with the project's ground rules: documentation is required for new features, and the app is built in Python and Django so that adding a scanner parser often takes only a small script. The REST API is usable through a Python library, though he admits it is rough. The stated goal is high-confidence reports with little human involvement, and he invites contributors. Version 1.2 had just been released.

talks.title: An Overview of API Underprotection
talks.teaser: Shows how public mobile apps expose API keys and tokens, and which defenses like TLS pinning and attestation help.
talks.summary:
The speaker opens by arguing that APIs have become central to how organisations and client apps communicate, and that the draft OWASP list at the time included a category for underprotected APIs. He sorts APIs into private, partner and public types, and notes that client designs have shifted logic into single-page and mobile apps, widening the attack surface.

Examples follow. A popular mobile game's private API was reverse engineered from captured traffic, and later checksum protections were broken quickly. An older Instagram password reset request could be tampered with through a proxy to return contact details for other accounts, enabling account takeover. He also covers injection risks, guessable endpoints, verb tampering and over-broad OAuth2 access tokens, plus traditional defenses such as rate limiting against application-layer denial of service and scraping.

The remainder focuses on software identity in public clients. Embedded API keys can be extracted, so a single client key with a proxy holding backend credentials is preferred, and signed tokens such as JWTs can carry expiry and claims. TLS alone does not stop a device with an added trust certificate from decoding traffic, so certificate pinning is needed despite its rotation costs. Stronger options include white box cryptography, app hardening, TrustZone and remote attestation. The key takeaway is to treat the API as the attack surface and combine user and software identity.

talks.title: Measuring End-to-End Security Engineering
talks.teaser: Shows how a security program can use bug postmortems, bounty-cost metrics and threat-model controls to prove it is working.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from the limits of common security program metrics such as bug counts, tool counts, training coverage and pen test coverage. A falling bug count can hide a weak program, and a rising one can reflect better discovery, so the speaker splits measurements into coverage, outputs and effectiveness. Because engineering teams are rewarded for shipping features rather than for reporting flaws, the approach also looks at when a bug was introduced, not only when it was found.

Every two weeks, a bug postmortem covers high and critical issues from customer reports, penetration tests and bug bounties. Each presentation records when the bug was born, what a bounty researcher would have been paid for it, the engineering and security time spent fixing it, and which part of the SDL failed, such as training, design, development or the pipeline. From these records the team tracks developer self-awareness, bounty cost per feature, bug survival time and process failure trends. A beta distribution, updated with vulnerable and clean features, estimates how many undiscovered bugs may still be in production.

For end-to-end security, the speaker walks through a threat model built from a PII inventory and service connections, with attacks mapped to controls and detections. Each control is weighed against the bounty it would reduce, and nightly validation tests check that controls keep working. A worked example of a calendar application shows how insecure upstream services add trusted bounty exposure. The talk closes with plans to automate the model, open-source parts of it and quantify risk. The main takeaway is to keep existing metrics but add cost-based measures that business leaders can understand.

talks.title: Juggling the Elephants: Making AppSec a Continuous Program
talks.teaser: Presents a model for running AppSec across large portfolios, linking risk ranking, assessments and design guidance.
talks.summary:
Tony Miller, a practice leader at a security consultancy, frames application security as a strategic problem for organizations with very large application portfolios. He describes the pressures involved: hundreds of applications, inconsistent risk views, shrinking budgets, pressure to ship faster in DevOps, and a constant stream of new technologies and threats. Rather than adding more one-off assessments, he proposes a model that connects several program components so they feed each other.

Profiling starts the model: business and technical traits, such as whether an app moves money, its internet exposure and its open-source use, feed a consistent risk ranking. That ranking sets the assessment strategy, choosing which activities such as threat modeling or code review apply to each application and how deeply. Reference architectures then give developers controls-focused design guidance, and self-service checks in the build pipeline let teams start testing without waiting on security staff.

The final stage uses analysis and metrics: vulnerability trends, design review findings and usage data refine risk scores, reference architectures and pen test cases. Miller also mapped the approach to seven SAMM practices and answered a question on legacy technology, where a reference architecture may cover only certain cases and assessments differ by deployment model. The takeaway is to profile applications, tie assessments to risk, and let program outputs drive continuous improvement.

talks.title: WAFs FTW! A modern devops approach to security testing your WAF
talks.teaser: Shows how the FTW framework turns web application firewall evaluation into repeatable, quantitative tests built on the OWASP Core Rule Set.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this presentation, speakers Christian Papathanasiou, Chaim Sanders, and Zack Allen introduce FTW (Framework for Testing WAFs), an open-source Python tool built on pytest to bring automated, quantitative testing and modern DevOps practices to Web Application Firewalls (WAFs). Evaluating WAF solutions has historically relied on qualitative, subjective assessments, such as Gartner Magic Quadrants, Forrester Waves, or OWASP WAFEC checklists, which fail to provide repeatable, data-driven guarantees about attack coverage, regression detection, or zero-day readiness. FTW solves this by formalizing attack payloads into structured YAML test definitions, enabling continuous integration testing across rule releases and edge deployments.

### Key Topics
- **Qualitative vs. Quantitative WAF Evaluation**: Traditional analyst reports and compliance checklists (e.g., PCI DSS checkboxes) do not prove whether a WAF reliably protects against nuanced attack variants. Quantifiable testing provides baseline metrics for vendor bake-offs and engineering validations.
- **FTW Architecture and Design**: Modeled after the Scapy network packet library, FTW automatically constructs baseline minimal HTTP/1.1 requests, allowing users to override specific attributes in human-readable YAML. Tests can intentionally violate RFCs (such as placing a message body on GET or HEAD requests) without being blocked by standard client libraries like curl or Python Requests.
- **DevOps Integration for OWASP CRS**: The OWASP Core Rule Set (CRS) project uses FTW inside Travis CI using Docker containers. As of CRS v3, all rule commits and pull requests require corresponding FTW test cases to prevent regressions.
- **Edge CDN Implementation at Fastly**: Fastly translates ModSecurity SecRules into Varnish Configuration Language (VCL) to run WAF logic directly at the edge. Fastly wrapped FTW in a custom test harness to verify behavior parity, validate regex ReDoS safety, and correlate injected test headers with WAF execution journals.

### Technical Details
FTW integrates with pytest to execute attack fixtures against target web applications or firewalls and verify expected HTTP status codes or log output. Key technical aspects include:
- **Non-RFC Compliant Payloads**: By crafting raw request streams, FTW can test rules like CRS 920170 (blocking GET/HEAD requests containing a `Content-Length` or request body), which standard HTTP client libraries prevent sending.
- **Fastly Translation & Validation Toolchain**: Fastly converts SecRules into VCL while preventing evasion bugs caused by discrepancies in request parsing or transform functions (e.g., lowercase conversions). Fastly's harness injects custom headers tracking rule timestamps and test IDs, reconciling journal logs with WAF logs to ensure payloads trigger the intended rule rather than failing on an unrelated check.
- **Vulnerabilities Identified and Fixed Upstream in CRS**:
  - *Restricted Extension Chaining Bug*: A protocol enforcement rule had a lowercase transformation applied in the wrong chain, allowing bypasses using uppercase file extensions like `.EXE`.
  - *Remote File Inclusion (RFI) Evasion*: The rule used a case-sensitive regex and missed the `file://` scheme, allowing bypasses via uppercase schemes like `HTTP://`.
  - *Session Fixation Flaw*: A rule used a `beginswith` operator comparing Referer and Host headers, which attackers could bypass using subdomains. The rule was corrected to use `endswith`.

### Takeaways
FTW transforms WAF testing from ad-hoc manual verification into repeatable CI/CD regression suites. Moving forward, the project roadmap includes developing YAML linters for rule authors, expanding negative testing by replaying traffic from top domains (e.g., Alexa top 1M) to reduce false positives, benchmarking cross-WAF performance, and maintaining community-accessible exploit tests for emerging vulnerabilities. FTW is open-source and installable via PyPI.

talks.title: An Agile Framework for Building GDPR Requirements into SDLC
talks.teaser: Shows how to tag GDPR articles and link them to agile user stories and privacy tasks for compliance tracking.
talks.summary:
Agile teams split work into epics, user stories and small tasks, which makes privacy impact assessments hard, because documentation is thin and nobody can see when every regulatory requirement is met. The talk separates two starting points: teams that must generate their own GDPR tasks from scratch, and teams that already work from a checklist of security and privacy tasks and need proof that together they achieve compliance.

The method borrows open, axial and selective coding from qualitative research. GDPR articles are tagged with a class and a variant, for example article 7 on consent and its withdrawal, and development tasks get the same tags, so tasks and articles connect through a shared tag rather than directly. Tagged articles become user stories, and stories sharing a goal are grouped into one epic; a breach notification epic joins a user's story and a supervisory authority's story. The speakers separate one-time feature requirements from recurring security controls, such as secure cookie flags and parameterized queries, which are easy to forget. A smart bracelet case study applied this to articles 7, 15, 17 and 34, and mapped design and testing tasks such as monitoring IoT devices for critical incidents.

For audits, the same tags can be applied as Jira labels, so an assessor can filter tagged tasks and check coverage. The SD Elements tool produces a task-level compliance report organised by article and recital. Practitioners can reuse the shared tags, user stories and mandate mappings as a starting point for their own agile projects.

talks.title: Androsia: A tool for securing in memory sensitive data
talks.teaser: Presents a static analyzer that clears sensitive in-memory data in Android apps right after its last use.
talks.summary:
Sensitive strings kept in memory can outlive their use, because garbage collection does not reliably erase them and developers may forget references that keep them alive. The talk introduces Androsia, a static analyzer for Android apps that targets StringBuilder objects and works out where each one is last used. It can either rewrite the app's bytecode to overwrite the contents at that point, or flag the spot so a developer can call a destroy method directly.

Underneath, the tool converts Dalvik bytecode into a three-address intermediate representation and runs a liveness analysis backwards through the program. Per-method summaries record the final use of local variables and static fields, and these are combined across callers so the last use is found at whole-program level. FlowDroid builds a synthetic main method so that lifecycle and UI callbacks share one entry point. Demonstrations showed how loops and static fields move the clearing point, and a heap dump of the instrumented app no longer contained the password. Support for instance fields was nearly finished, with a test suite and CI integration still planned.

The main takeaway is that relying on the garbage collector is not enough, and that clearing sensitive data at its last use is a practical defence. The code was still private at the time of the talk while the speaker's employer approved its release as open source.

talks.title: Enhancing Physical Perimeter Defense Using SDR
talks.teaser: Shows how a software-defined radio can log nearby phone identifiers to spot unfamiliar devices around a home or office perimeter.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that perimeter defenses built around cameras and motion sensors miss a useful signal: most people who approach a home or office carry a cell phone. The speaker proposes using a software-defined radio to record the identifiers, timestamps and signal strengths of nearby mobile devices. A low-power GSM base station, run every five to ten minutes at deliberately limited power, is used to prompt phones to reveal themselves. Hardware options range from cheap receive-only TV dongles to faster USB 3.0 radios that can transmit, and pricier Ethernet-connected units.

The captured records are then grouped by pattern. Regular residents show steady presence, while deliveries, gardeners and commuters appear for short, predictable windows. A device never seen before, or one that lingers close to the property at an unusual hour, deserves attention. The speaker walked through simulated data sets to show how these patterns separate a neighbour, a commuter, a gardener and a possible intruder, and noted that the data shown was not from real people.

The speaker also covered ways to reduce false positives, such as checking alerts against camera footage or sending a drone on a patrol route. Limits include phones that are hidden, powered off or shielded, and signal strength being an unreliable distance estimate. Operating GSM spectrum may also break regulations, so experiments should stay in a controlled setting. The main takeaway is that logging device identifiers can support investigation alongside existing sensors rather than replace them.

talks.title: How To Approach InfoSec Like a Fed(eral Auditor)
talks.teaser: Explains how FIPS 140-2 and Common Criteria requirements translate into five design principles for web and IoT developers.
talks.summary:
The talk compares two US government security standards, FIPS 140-2 for cryptographic modules and Common Criteria for IT products, and distills five principles that web application and IoT developers can apply. The speaker explains that FIPS matters for selling cryptographic products to federal systems, while Common Criteria applies to IT products bought by the DoD.

The first principle is to define a security boundary around all software, firmware or hardware, plus every physical port and logical interface that crosses it. Listing these exposes undocumented entry points, third-party parts and leftover test code. The second is a functional specification explaining why each interface exists, so unneeded functions get questioned. For the crypto-focused principles, a sample key management document tracks each critical security parameter, including random generator inputs and authentication data, and how each is protected and destroyed.

The talk then urges encrypting internal management traffic such as LDAP and syslog, validating x.509 certificates on every connection instead of trusting libraries, and checking the strength of every algorithm in context. An RSA 2048 key or a weak Diffie-Hellman group can cap a TLS connection below AES-128 strength, and low entropy can undermine a generated key. The closing advice is to define the boundary, measure real security strength, and test crypto libraries rather than assume they work.

talks.title: Building Secure ASP.NET Core MVC Applications
talks.teaser: AppSecUSA 2017 analyzes Building Secure ASP.NET Core MVC Applications.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this talk, Niels Tanis examines the security landscape of ASP.NET Core MVC compared to legacy ASP.NET MVC. Because ASP.NET Core MVC is a modular, multi-platform total rewrite, it introduces new conventions, dependency injection by default, and safer baseline configurations. Tanis focuses on how data is processed, returned, and protected, specifically evaluating common web vulnerabilities such as Cross-Site Scripting (XSS), Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF), and mass assignment/over-posting.

### Key Topics
- **Controller Discovery and Routing Conventions**: In ASP.NET Core MVC, controllers are identified by convention (any class ending with the name `Controller`), requiring no explicit base class inheritance. This behavior means any loaded assembly could unintentionally expose controllers unless restricted via the `ApplicationPartManager`.
- **Data Ingestion and State Management**: Tanis underscores that HTTP GET requests must never modify internal application state. For write operations, actions must be restricted to HTTP POST and protected against CSRF.
- **Over-Posting and Mass Assignment**: Directly binding external input to ORM entity models can result in over-posting attacks (e.g., overwriting sensitive properties like `TotalPrice`). Defenses include whitelisting with the `[Bind]` attribute, using predicates in `TryUpdateModelAsync`, or preferably, using dedicated ViewModel request/response classes.
- **Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) Defenses**: The framework defaults to safer content types (`text/plain` rather than `text/html`) when returning strings. Razor views automatically HTML-encode values unless developers explicitly bypass protection with `Html.Raw` or `HtmlString`.
- **SameSite Cookie Integration**: Tanis details how SameSite cookies (`Lax` and `Strict`) mitigate CSRF and cross-origin resource leakage side-channels, and highlights how ASP.NET Core 2.0 introduced `CookiePolicyMiddleware` to automate SameSite policies.
- **Roslyn Code Analysis**: Static analysis rules built on the Roslyn compiler platform can parse controller syntax trees to ensure security patterns are followed.

### Technical Details
- **Anti-Forgery Protections**: Methods can be decorated with `[ValidateAntiForgeryToken]`, or developers can globally configure an `AutoValidateAntiforgeryTokenAttribute` filter within `ConfigureServices` in the `Startup` class. ASP.NET Core tag helpers automatically append anti-forgery tokens to generated forms.
- **Encoding Services**: The built-in dependency injection container exposes contextual encoders derived from the AntiXSS library (`HtmlEncoder`, `JavaScriptEncoder`, `UrlEncoder`), allowing programmatic output encoding without manual instantiation.
- **Cookie Authentication Options**: Tanis demonstrates replacing the default cookie manager in `CookieAuthenticationOptions` with a custom implementation to append `SameSite=Lax`. In ASP.NET Core 2.0, the framework sets `SameSite=Lax` for session cookies and `SameSite=Strict` for anti-forgery cookies by default.
- **Roslyn AST Validation**: Tanis details custom Roslyn-based checks iterating through controller methods to verify: (1) if an action has `[HttpPost]`, it also possesses `[ValidateAntiForgeryToken]`; and (2) action method bodies explicitly evaluate `ModelState.IsValid` before persisting data.

### Takeaways
While ASP.NET Core MVC provides significantly improved secure-by-default behaviors compared to classic MVC, developers must remain vigilant. Critical fundamentals like explicit HTTP verb binding, input validation with data annotations, ViewModels to prevent mass assignment, and context-aware output encoding remain necessary. Automated AST analysis via Roslyn offers an accessible mechanism to enforce these baseline requirements across application codebases.

talks.title: Keynote - Tony UcedaVelez - Fixing Threat Models with OWASP Efforts
talks.teaser: AppSecUSA 2017 investigates Tony UcedaVelez - Fixing Threat Models with OWASP Efforts.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this keynote address at an OWASP conference in Orlando, Tony UcedaVelez discusses the persistent dysfunctions in threat modeling and application security, arguing that security organizations rely too heavily on automated scanning tools and compliance checklists without understanding threat intelligence or actual business impact. Drawing from consulting experiences with federal agencies, medical IoT startups, and commercial insurers, he urges practitioners to move away from post-implementation bug hunting and adopt risk-centric threat modeling early in the software development lifecycle (SDLC) by weaponizing existing OWASP tools and frameworks.

### Key Topics
- **Communication Breakdown & The Risk Formula**: Security professionals often struggle to articulate business value. The traditional formula $\text{Risk} = \text{Threat} \times \text{Vulnerability} \times \text{Impact}$ is often misused because organizations focus almost exclusively on finding bugs (vulnerabilities) through SAST, DAST, IAST, and RASP tools while ignoring realistic threats and the financial impact on operations.
- **The PASTA Framework**: As co-author of the Process for Attack Simulation and Threat Analysis (PASTA), UcedaVelez highlights its seven stages, emphasizing Stage 1 (Business Impact) and Stage 4 (Threat Intelligence). Unlike generic checklists, PASTA models risk by incorporating real adversary motivations, incident precedents, and operational consequences.
- **Evidentiary Threat Modeling vs. Generic Lists**: The OWASP Top 10 or standard lists should not be treated as a complete threat model. Effective models require decomposing application architectures, inspecting protocols (such as CoAP and DTLS in IoT), evaluating trust boundaries, and building attack trees or attack patterns (referencing CAPEC) grounded in actual threat data.
- **Aligning Security with Business Value**: Translating technical security findings into monetary impact—such as financial losses per hour of downtime, regulatory penalties, or compromised records—transforms security requirements into functional priorities that developers and executives can support.

### Technical Details
- **Application Decomposition & Protocols**: Practitioners must understand underlying protocols and RFC specifications rather than treating applications as black boxes. For example, when assessing lightweight IoT protocols like CoAP that run over UDP rather than TCP/TLS, security engineers must evaluate mitigations like DTLS.
- **Mapping OWASP Projects to Threat Modeling Stages**:
  - *Stage 1 (Business Impact)*: OWASP CISO Project metrics help derive financial impact and justify security investments.
  - *Preemptive Hardening*: OWASP Cheat Sheets and the Application Security Verification Standard (ASVS) provide baseline mitigation before deep modeling.
  - *Stages 4 & 5 (Threat & Vulnerability Identification)*: Combining threat intelligence with tools like OWASP ZAP and the OWASP Testing Guide to evaluate specific weakness points.
  - *Stage 6 (Attack Modeling)*: Using frameworks such as the OWASP Web Testing Framework (WTF), PTES (Penetration Testing Execution Standard), and the ModSecurity Core Rule Set (alongside WAF benchmarking) to simulate probabilistic, criminal-style attack paths rather than running automated scanner scripts blindly.
  - *Maturity & Governance*: Utilizing OpenSAMM (and referencing BSIMM) to iteratively mature software security programs.

### Takeaways
- **Shift Left with Empathy**: Stop acting as "collectors" delivering tickets after deployment; engage developers early during architectural design to avoid costly remediation cycles.
- **Speak the Business Language**: Communicate security risk in terms of revenue, operational uptime, and regulatory consequences rather than raw vulnerability names.
- **Operationalize Community Resources**: Utilize OWASP's extensive ecosystem (ASVS, ZAP, CISO Project, Juice Shop, OpenSAMM) to implement an evidence-based, threat-informed security program.

talks.title: HUNT: Data Driven Web Hacking & Manual Testing - JP Villanueva
talks.teaser: Shows a Burp Suite extension that flags risky parameters from bug bounty data and guides manual web testing.
talks.summary:
The talk introduces HUNT, a Burp Suite extension built to help web application testers work through large, dynamic sites by hand. It targets three gaps: applications with hundreds of parameters are hard to cover manually, newer testers often lack the experience to know where bugs hide, and Burp has no built-in workflow for methodology and reporting.

The scanner draws on data from more than 600 bug bounty programs, about 18,000 parameters in all, filtered down to those tied to critical and high severity findings and sorted by how often names recurred. Parameters are grouped by vulnerability class: ID-style names point toward SQL injection and insecure direct object references, file and locale names toward file includes, redirect-style names toward SSRF, and access or debug flags toward logic bypasses. The passive scanner raises these as traffic passes through Burp, with advisories and reference links. Checkboxes track what has been tested, and duplicate hits are suppressed.

The methodology window lets testers send a request and response pair into a matching step, such as account functionality, and keep bug entries, resources and notes in one place. Sessions save and load as JSON, which can feed a report or be passed to a more senior tester. Both lists can be extended by editing JSON, and planned work includes REST support and more methodologies. The main takeaway is that HUNT speeds up manual testing rather than replacing it, and testers should dig into error responses rather than stop at them.

talks.title: ReproNow: Save time Reproducing and Triaging Security bugs
talks.teaser: Shows how a browser extension records screen and network traffic so bug reports can be reproduced and triaged faster.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at how long bug bounty submissions take to triage. Security engineers often have to reproduce a reported issue by hand, and back-and-forth requests for HTTP traces, screenshots, or video can stretch resolution times and frustrate researchers. The speakers frame this as a workflow problem tied to language gaps, product knowledge gaps, and long, complex reports.

They present ReproNow, an open-source browser extension for Chrome and Opera, with Firefox support in progress. It records the screen and network traffic locally, using getUserMedia for capture and the webRequest API for logging, because the debugger API would show a warning bar. The network log is embedded as an attachment inside an MKV file that still plays in ordinary video players. A companion previewer syncs requests with the video, supports search, and exports requests as curl commands or to Burp. A live demo showed a SQL injection test against a login page being recorded, reviewed, and exported.

Limitations were acknowledged: response bodies are not captured with the webRequest API, and simultaneous recording of two separate browser sessions is not supported yet. The speakers argue that a replayable recording lets engineers confirm a bug quickly, check whether a fix holds, or test other browsers, and can help scanners that struggle with login flows. Questions about malicious attachments were answered by noting the viewer is plain JavaScript that runs client-side.

talks.teaser: Learn how scope, staffing, disclosure, and payment choices shape a bug bounty program.
talks.summary: The panel discusses how companies can set up and run bug bounty programs, including public and private models, scope, researcher incentives, payments, disclosure, and legal risks. Panelists describe how bounties fit alongside scanning and penetration testing, and why clear internal ownership, communication, and processes for triaging and fixing reports matter. Attendees learn practical considerations for choosing a program model and setting expectations with researchers and engineering teams.

talks.title: Passive Fingerprinting of HTTP/2 Clients - Elad Shuster
talks.teaser: Shows how HTTP/2 settings, priority and header order can fingerprint software clients passively.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at HTTP/2 as a binary protocol that is almost always carried over TLS, which makes it hard to inspect by hand. It opens with usage figures from a large CDN platform, where HTTP/2 made up roughly a tenth of traffic, and then walks through the protocol's building blocks: frames, streams and messages. It also covers the changes from HTTP/1, including multiplexing within one TCP connection, HPACK header compression and server push.

The core of the talk is passive client fingerprinting. Nothing is injected into the client. Instead, the attributes a client sends when it opens a connection are recorded. The chosen elements are the SETTINGS frame parameters, the initial WINDOW_UPDATE value, the PRIORITY tree that some clients build at startup, and the order of pseudo-headers in the first request. Examples show that Firefox, Safari, Chrome on Android, curl and common libraries each produce distinct combinations. The research drew on about 10 million HTTP/2 connections and over 40,000 user agents, though a single fingerprint can still cover several browsers or versions.

Use cases include spotting browser impersonators and automated tools that claim a user agent they do not match. Another is flagging IPs that show many distinct fingerprints, which may point to a proxy, VPN or corporate gateway. The speaker stresses combining application-layer fingerprints with TCP and TLS attributes to add entropy. The talk closes by noting that HTTP/2 attacks are still rare, since most common testing tools lack support, but that attention to the protocol is growing.

talks.title: AppSecUSA 2017 Leaders Session
talks.teaser: Covers OWASP chapter governance, dispute handling, and planned tool moves from mailing lists to Discourse.
talks.summary:
This AppSecUSA 2017 leaders session, aimed at OWASP chapter and project leaders, opens with the community's compliance committee, which mediates disputes between members. Its scope covers conflicts such as bullying, misused chapter funds, or ethics violations. Staff disputes go to the executive director, and board matters fall into a grey area. Leaders are asked to try resolving problems locally first, because complaints that reach the committee move slowly, and a case that enters the legal system stops the committee's process.

The second half covers organizational change. Staff capacity is temporarily reduced, and the organization is moving from ad hoc growth toward a stronger foundation. Planned changes include replacing the unsupported Mailman lists with a Discourse forum, rolled out in phases starting with a small chapter and project pilot. Chapter Meetup groups are also moving to Meetup Pro so the organization keeps control of shared assets. Discussion covered limiting each chapter or project to three leaders, and keeping leadership records documented and current.

Vendor influence was the next topic. Attendees described sponsor pitches taking over chapter meetings and sponsor-funded talks drifting into sales. Suggested responses included capping sponsor time and diversifying leadership. Funding options for projects, such as community outreach money and grants, were also covered. The session closed by collecting feedback and encouraging members to take part in the board election.

talks.title: AppSecUSA 2016 - Keynote - Sammy Kamkar - The Less Hacked Path
talks.teaser: Recounts a MySpace worm and a tour of side-channel attacks that leak data through sound, light and power.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with the speaker's teenage years, when a Windows 95 denial-of-service tool and a Counter-Strike cheat pushed him toward programming. At 19 he altered a MySpace profile with a script that spread to roughly a million profiles before the site took it down. He describes the investigators who searched his home and the years of computer restrictions that followed.

The middle of the talk covers later research. He built Skyjack, an open project that took over nearby consumer drones over wireless and turned them into a swarm under his control. He also showed how location data leaks through Street View Wi-Fi scans and phone collection of nearby router information. His side-channel examples included keystrokes recovered from a laser bounced off a laptop, from microphone and accelerometer data, and from ground-line noise, plus a 496-bit RSA key extracted from an Android phone's ultrasound. Smaller cases included a chip-and-pin card overlay, magstripe emulation, and a Mattel toy with a radio chip used to open garage doors.

He closes by urging attendees to think through low-cost attacks before buying security gadgets, and to weigh layered defenses against the risk they accept. In the Q&A he recommended learning to code as the strongest path into security, because writing tools exposes the same logic errors that attackers exploit.

talks.title: AppSecUSA 2016 - Keynote - Matthew Green - Cryptography in the age of Heartbleed
talks.teaser: Traces how TLS flaws, export ciphers and confusing crypto APIs cause real breaks, and what developers should do instead.
talks.summary:
The keynote argues that cryptography now matters directly to application developers, since weak crypto can undermine software that relies on secure connections. It opens with Heartbleed and the goto fail bug, then traces the history of SSL and TLS from its 1994 origins through the rename to TLS and the current TLS 1.2. Backward compatibility explains why old protocol versions and export-grade ciphers linger.

A network attacker can strip strong cipher suites from a client's offer, leaving a 512-bit RSA export key that takes about an hour and roughly $70 on EC2 to factor. Scanning found that more than 30 percent of servers still accepted export encryption, including government sites. Several TLS implementations also shared one browser-side bug that let clients accept export keys they never requested. Library design came in for heavy criticism: OpenSSL's interfaces, Java cipher defaults that may fall back to ECB mode, unauthenticated encryption, RSA PKCS#1 v1.5, a confusing Microsoft certificate-validation call, and curl options that switch off verification.

A Juniper NetScreen case showed that a backdoor can be planted by altering a 32-byte value in shipped code. The speaker recommends higher-level libraries such as NaCl or libsodium, whose simple functions remove many choices from developers. The closing message is that crypto is hard, but recent attention may push the field toward better tools.

talks.title: AppSec EU 2017 LT Is Software Eating Security? by Dave Anderson
talks.teaser: Explores how software-driven transformation reshapes security roles, tools, and collaboration across modern organizations.
talks.summary:
The presenter argues that security professionals must reckon with transformation that arrives gradually rather than through a single planned change. Inspiration comes from writing on tidal forces in insecurity, alongside metaphors about unprepared responses to sudden scale and cultural shifts. He contrasts yesterday’s hand-sized architecture sketches with today’s microservice graphs, constant event streams, daily releases, CI/CD pipelines, containers, and chaos testing, noting that complexity and speed widen attack surfaces faster than older endpoint and scanning models assume.

Mobile devices, SaaS email and backups, fewer on-prem servers, and cloud enthusiasm erode assumptions behind many traditional controls. Silos between business, development, security, operations, and test remain destructive; he questions simplistic shift-left rhetoric in favor of including security throughout delivery, while cautioning that isolated central teams cannot keep pace. Running software in the public cloud without genuine cloud-native behavior offers little real progress.

He urges asking why work is done, clarifying core competencies as technology evolves, and joining integrated product teams rather than peripheral IT functions. Closing guidance favors secure development, security champions, framing issues as defects, educating teams through mixed formal and hands-on learning, immutable and event-driven designs with limited blast radius, automated security-by-design thinking, and collaborative threat modeling before features ship.

talks.title: AppSec EU 2017 LT How To Ensure That No One Wants To Work With You by Siren Hofvander
talks.teaser: Outlines cultural barriers that push newcomers away from security and recommends welcoming hires, readable policy, and broader skill norms.
talks.summary:
The presentation grew from a friend’s discouraging experience at several security conferences, where aggressive personalities made the field feel unwelcoming despite genuine interest. The speaker frames three structural problems: conferences and career paths split “policy people” and “techies,” Hollywood and hacker events over-glorify penetration testing while undervaluing other roles, and hiring posts label jobs entry-level yet demand long experience and heavy certification stacks.

On the policy side, the talk argues that ISO-style documents matter for auditors but fail users who never read or remember them. A practical fix is pairing auditor-facing policy with short, role-specific guidance people can actually retain. For technologists, the Bose headphones privacy story illustrates violations buried in terms of service that code-focused testing would miss, pushing the audience to respect logical and privacy issues outside exploit demos.

Closing recommendations include mentoring, creating real junior roles, running beginner-only meetups such as the speaker’s Stockholm group, and accepting diverse opinions without conference or social-media pile-ons. A brief Q&A reinforces hiring for bravery and tailoring policy length to the problem each role must solve.
